Ocasio-Cortez Says She Is Freezing Her Eggs and Still Mulling a Presidential Run

The New York Times August 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In a TV interview, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez distanced herself from positions like “defund the police” and indicated she hasn’t ruled out a presidential or Senate run.

By Chelsia Rose Marcius and Bayliss Wagner

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York posted a series of video clips on social media Saturday night saying that she would freeze her eggs despite what she called a “political risk” for sharing her decision.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, 36, a Democrat who represents parts of Queens and the Bronx, made the announcement hours before saying in a TV interview Sunday that she is open to running for president or the Senate.

“There is very strangely a political risk, or a political tax, that comes with sharing this info,” she said of her decision to freeze her eggs. She added that she had shared the information “to show more depictions of women having full lives in every context and every choice.” The announcement further fueled speculation on social media that she is gearing up for a presidential run.

Asked on ABC News’s “This Week” on Sunday morning if she would consider a White House bid, she said, “I haven’t ruled out the possibility,” adding that she was “humbled” by the support she is receiving.

She also suggested she would consider running for the Senate seat held by the minority leader, Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, telling host Jonathan Karl that “anything is possible at this juncture.” But, she added, “I think that we have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations or plans.”

Her interview Sunday — her first appearance on a major Sunday news show since 2024 — marked her most public suggestion yet of aspirations for higher office. First elected in 2018, she rapidly became a top voice in her party’s ascendant progressive wing.

While Ms. Ocasio-Cortez identifies as a democratic socialist, she distanced herself in the interview from some of the more radical positions of the Democratic Socialists of America. Asked if she supports all of the tenets of the group’s guiding document, including abolishing the Senate, police and prisons, she said no. She also said she was a member of her local D. S. A. chapter, but not the national group.

The comments reflected the somewhat tricky position Ms. Ocasio-Cortez finds herself in this year. She has adopted a less confrontational style in her years in Congress, and in some ways, she is more moderate now than the progressive base that propelled her into office. Yet she still needs that base as she eyes her political future.

Asked if she believed the D. S. A.’s agenda would “doom” Democrats, she said, “The idea that there’s a diversity of thought in America among everyday voting people is a fundamental fact of our country. I don’t think that we should be worried about what somebody somewhere believes.”

On social media, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez described her ability to freeze her eggs as a “very privileged position.”

“And it’s also a result of I think changes in technology that have made it more financially accessible,” she added.

In her interview with ABC News on Sunday morning, the congresswoman elaborated on her announcement, calling it “badass that I’m going to be giving myself shots in the green room.”

“In this political environment, where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations,” she said.

As of noon on Sunday, neither President Trump nor any of her colleagues in Congress had responded to her announcement on social media.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who supports abortion rights, has been vocal regarding her stance on reproductive rights. In July 2022, the House of Representatives passed the Women’s Health Protection Act, a bill she sponsored to codify abortion rights into federal law after the Supreme Court decision to overturn Roe v. Wade. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez and several other members of Congress were arrested the same month at an abortion rights rally outside the Supreme Court in Washington.

In her comments about freezing her eggs, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez did not specify whether she plans to have children. But she indicated that she has faced questions about her family plans that her male colleagues have not.

“This is just not something that men deal with,” she said in one of her Instagram videos. “Men run for office, or frankly they interview for jobs. And people don’t think in the back of their minds, OK, this guy’s running for office, how old is he, oh, well, is he going to want to start a family?”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez and Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, led the field of potential Democratic presidential contenders in a poll of New Hampshire voters in the University of New Hampshire’s “Granite State Poll” of 648 likely voters in July.

Discussing her political future on Sunday, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez also reflected on her past and that of her party.

She neither distanced herself from nor explicitly supported Hasan Piker, the left-wing streamer who has faced criticism for once saying that America “deserved” the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. (Mr. Piker later walked back the remark.) But she said her fellow Democratic candidates should seek to appeal to audiences across the political spectrum, including both the far left and the far right.

“We need to be not so willing to engage in cancel culture,” she said. “Democrats can go on Joe Rogan, Democrats can go on Fox News. Democrats have a responsibility to build a winning coalition, and young people are engaging in mediums and conversations that we have a responsibility to attend to and be responsive to.”

She distanced herself from her own past support for such left-wing positions as defunding the police, attributing some of those positions, some of them deeply polarizing, to the political fervor that seized Democrats during the COVID era.

Asked whether the left went too far, however, she said the discussions at that time were “fruitful.”

“The doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place,” she said. “Of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today, and I’m grateful that these candidates have the opportunity to present who they are to their electorate and what they’re campaigning on in this moment.”

Egg freezing can be a lengthy, expensive process that is not always covered by health insurance. It requires women to inject two to three hormone medications every day for roughly 10 days, according to Johns Hopkins Medicine.

Women must also have at least four pelvic ultrasounds and frequent bloodwork panels. When the eggs mature, women undergo surgery to retrieve them. Despite the arduous process, it often fails.

AOC isn't the first Congresswoman to speak publicly about freezing her eggs. Rep. Sara Jacobs, Democrat of California, told my colleague Annie Karni that she did so last summer, saying that she was "the busiest I’ve ever been in this job." https://www. nytimes. com/2025/09/08/us/politics/sara-jacobs-egg-freezing-pregnancy-bill. html

In her interview with ABC, the congresswoman also echoed a viral comment from a New York City council member, Chi Ossé: “Woke one was crazy.” The phrase refers to left-leaning policy positions from the COVID era. Ossé first posted it in May when asked to address his statement in 2021 that a “cis white man should not be the next speaker of the Council.”

Chelsia Rose Marcius is a criminal justice reporter for The Times, covering the New York Police Department.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Mother and Daughter Die After Boat Overturns in New York Harbor

The New York Times August 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Police divers found a 27-year-old woman and her 5-month-old baby in the water near Liberty Island. A man was arrested and charged with reckless endangerment.

By Leo Sands and Davaughnia Wilson

A man was arrested and charged on Sunday with reckless endangerment after a 27-year-old woman and her 5-month-old daughter died when a boat he was operating overturned in New York Harbor, the Police Department said.

Emergency responders received a 911 call at approximately 10:25 p. m. on Saturday reporting an overturned vessel near Liberty Island, in Upper New York Bay, according to a police statement. Manuel Hernandez, 46, who was the captain of the boat, was arrested and charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment, the police said.

After deploying an air-and-sea helicopter rescue unit to the scene, police divers found the woman, Sara Sanchez, and infant, Antonella Garcia, in the water in critical condition, officials said. The police transported the victims to NYU Langone Hospital in Brooklyn, where they were later pronounced dead. Ms. Sanchez was from Queens, according to the police.

Officials said 12 other people were rescued from the bay before the police arrived at the scene and were transported to hospitals in the area with minor injuries. They remain in stable condition. Adam Schwartz, the owner of Sea the City, a tour and jet ski rental company, said that one of his boats was the first on the scene and rescued 11 people.

The U. S. Coast Guard, which also responded to the incident, is working with the Police Department to determine whether the incident involved an illegal charter operation.

“We are committed to holding illegal operators accountable to highest extent of the law to ensure the safety of everyone on our waterways,” said Captain Doreen McCarthy, head of the New York sector for the Coast Guard.

An illegal charter is any recreational or for hire vessel that lacks Coast Guard credentials, safety equipment, or certificate of inspection.

No other boats were believed to be involved in the incident, the police said.

According to the National Data Buoy Center, there was a moderate breeze in the area at the time, with wind speeds of 14 knots (around 16 miles per hour) recorded at 10:24 p. m.

The deadly incident echoed a similar summertime boating accident in July 2022, when a 27-foot boat capsized in the Hudson River near Midtown Manhattan, leaving two people dead including a 7-year-old boy.

Leo Sands is a correspondent for the Breaking News Hub of The New York Times based in London.

Davaughnia Wilson is a news assistant at The Times who helps to cover the New York City region.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s call with the former president comes as he tries to win over wary Democrats in Michigan’s high-stakes Senate race.

By Tim Balk and Bayliss Wagner

Tim Balk reported from Detroit.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed spoke by phone with former President Barack Obama on Friday, days after winning the Democratic primary race for Senate in Michigan, according to their representatives.

Mr. Obama and Dr. El-Sayed, who narrowly prevailed in a divisive primary after campaigning on a progressive and anti-establishment platform, discussed unifying the party before the November general election in Michigan, Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign said.

The call with Mr. Obama, who is selective in his outreach to up-and-coming Democrats, was one of many between prominent Democrats and Dr. El-Sayed after he defeated Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate backed by party leaders in Washington, after a bitter race.

Mr. Obama also called Ms. Stevens on Friday and discussed uniting the party, according to a person briefed on the conversation. Politico previously reported on that conversation.

Dr. El-Sayed’s race against former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee, could determine control of the Senate.

In TV interviews on Sunday morning, Dr. El-Sayed expressed appreciation for Mr. Obama’s outreach. He told CNN’s “State of the Union” that it that it had been a “really, really warm conversation,” and an honor.

And he told “Meet the Press” that he “really” hoped Mr. Obama would campaign with him, noting that the former president “knows a lot about winning Michigan.” Mr. Obama carried the state in 2008 and 2012.

Since the primary, Dr. El-Sayed has also spoken with Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader; former Vice President Kamala Harris; and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York, among others. (Mr. Schumer, who had endorsed Ms. Stevens, said in an interview with The New York Times that he had told Dr. El-Sayed, “I don’t need you to like me, I just need you to win,” an account that Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign confirmed.)

He has spoken more than once with Ms. Stevens, who has endorsed him.

During the primary race, Mr. Obama did not endorse either Dr. El-Sayed or Ms. Stevens. But allies of Ms. Stevens pointed often to her work leading the Obama administration’s auto task force, and they spent millions running ads that showed him praising her during her 2018 run for the House of Representatives.

Dr. El-Sayed, who ran for governor in 2018 and could become the first Muslim senator if he wins in November, has at times been compared to Mr. Obama over the years. Both men are skilled orators. And both of their fathers immigrated to the United States from Africa. (Mr. Obama’s father came from Kenya, Dr. El-Sayed’s from Egypt.)

On Sunday, Dr. El-Sayed recalled watching Mr. Obama’s speech at the 2004 Democratic National Convention as a college student and seeing politics in a new light.

“I never saw myself in politics until I saw him give that 2004 speech on the D. N. C. floor,” Dr. El-Sayed told the CNN host Jake Tapper.

At times, though, Dr. El-Sayed has also pushed back on comparisons to Mr. Obama.

“I’m very thankful for what he was able to change in our politics about who could and couldn’t aspire to leadership,” Dr. El-Sayed told Vox in 2017. But he added that there were “a lot of things I disagree with President Obama on — in terms of both domestic and, certainly, international politics. I’m not him, and I have no intention of being him.”

In his 2020 book “Healing Politics,” Dr. El-Sayed wrote that Mr. Obama’s presidency in part represented “inspiring intentions unfulfilled.”

After the call, though, Dr. El-Sayed did not seem to be dwelling on their disagreements.

“Sometimes,” he said in a statement, “you really should meet your heroes.”

Michael Kruse contributed reporting.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Iran Elevates Longtime Military Commander to Top Security Post

The New York Times August 09, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The appointment of Mohsen Rezaei as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council suggests that Iran’s old guard is consolidating power.

By Yeganeh Torbati

Iran is replacing its top national security adviser with a longtime military commander whose appointment could represent a further consolidation of power by the country’s old-guard security establishment.

Mohsen Rezaei, who led Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps during the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, will be the new secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, a spokesman for Iran’s president wrote on social media on Sunday.

He had been serving as an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.

Mr. Rezaei is replacing Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who stepped into the role when the council’s previous secretary, Ali Larijani, was killed in an Israeli strike during the U. S.-Israeli attacks on Iran earlier this year.

Seyed Mehdi Tabatabaei, a spokesman for President Masoud Pezeshkian, said on social media that Mr. Zolghadr had resigned, would take up a new position, and that Mr. Rezaei would take his place.

While Mr. Zolghadr is himself a veteran of the Revolutionary Guards, Iran’s most powerful security force, analysts say he does not have the authority of some other current and former senior military commanders.

The council, which includes top civilian and military officials, plays a critical role in deciding Iranian policy on the ongoing conflict with the United States. It agreed in June to a memorandum of understanding that would pause the war, although that agreement quickly fell apart because of disputes between the United States and Iran about control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Hamidreza Azizi, a Berlin-based expert on Iranian security issues, said Mr. Rezaei’s appointment was significant for several reasons.

For one, it signaled that the country’s longtime security chiefs were further entrenching their power rather than making way for a transition toward a younger generation of political elites, he said. Mr. Rezaei has been a constant in the highest levels of Iran’s military and politics for over four decades. In addition to his military role, he ran for president several times, unsuccessfully.

Mr. Azizi said the appointment also indicated an effort to counterbalance Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has been leading Iran’s negotiations with the United States. Mr. Ghalibaf, another veteran Guards commander, is the speaker of Parliament and known to be close to Mr. Zolghadr. The turnover at the top of the security council could represent a balancing act by Ayatollah Khamenei “to prevent the excessive influence of Ghalibaf,” Mr. Azizi said.

Mr. Ghalibaf has in the past defended the cease-fire agreement that Iran struck with the United States in June, even as more hard-line elements within the country attacked the deal. Mr. Rezaei’s appointment, Mr. Azizi said, “would mean that the more hard-line side of the system is getting the upper hand.”

Saeid Golkar, a professor at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga who studies Iran’s security forces, said Mr. Rezaei’s elevation was a further sign that the Revolutionary Guards were making the key decisions within Iran.

But in Mr. Golkar’s view, this change does not indicate that those decisions would be more hard-line, or more pragmatic for that matter.

What does seem likely, he said, is that Mr. Rezaei and Mr. Ghalibaf would eventually clash because of their intense ambitions. Like Mr. Rezaei, Mr. Ghalibaf has run for the presidency in the past. “This configuration is not going to work,” Mr. Golkar said. “Everybody wants to be a king.”

Officially, Iran’s president appoints the secretary of the council. In practice, however, the supreme leader decides who fills the post, Mr. Golkar said.

In videotaped comments shared widely on social media last week, Mohammad Bagher Kharrazi — a hard-line cleric related by marriage to Ayatollah Khamenei — anticipated the appointment and framed it as part of an effort to rein in Iran’s president, Mr. Pezeshkian. Mr. Pezeshkian and his foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, have been harshly attacked by Iranian hard-liners over their efforts at diplomacy with the United States.

In Mr. Kharrazi’s telling, Mr. Pezeshkian has repeatedly threatened to resign as president to get his way, and Ayatollah Khamenei, the supreme leader, has grown impatient and warned him he would accept his next such offer.

To further restrain the president, Ayatollah Khamenei was also working on changing the security council, planning to remove “Mr. Zolghadr and having Mr. Mohsen Rezaei take his place,” Mr. Kharrazi said. He also said that Ayatollah Khamenei had told Mr. Araghchi that “under no circumstances does he have the right to interfere in the negotiations anymore.”

Ayatollah Khamenei’s office, without naming Mr. Kharrazi, denied the account, as did Mr. Pezeshkian’s office.

Yeganeh Torbati is the Iran correspondent for The Times.

Iran, Holding Firm to Strait, Steers Trump Back to June Deal

The New York Times August 09, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

The Strait of Hormuz is Iran’s best leverage to get Washington to release Iran’s frozen assets, lift economic sanctions and end its naval blockade.

By Steven Erlanger

Steven Erlanger, based in Berlin, has written about Iran and the Middle East since the Iranian Revolution.

Iran’s demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as laid out in a statement on Saturday, are largely what President Trump had already agreed to do in the memorandum of understanding that was signed on June 17 and quickly fell apart. But Iran sees control over the strait as its best chance of getting Mr. Trump to deliver on those promises — and is not willing to give it up just yet.

For Iran, analysts suggest, denying Mr. Trump the ability to claim victory over the strait is the most efficient lever to persuade him to recommit to those agreements and to implement them. Keeping the strait largely closed keeps energy prices high and is also a way to ensure that Persian Gulf states, which depend on the strait for exports, will also encourage Washington to return to the memorandum.

The level of mistrust between Iran and the United States is so high that Tehran wants to ensure it gets the economic relief it has been promised, to enable reconstruction, before it gives up even partial control over the strait, said Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, founder of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, a think tank focused on economic diplomacy.

“Iranian officials are concerned that if the strait opens, Trump would walk away from this conflict without feeling the need to resolve it,” he said. “They want to use the strait as a commitment mechanism to ensure Trump implements the various provisions of the MOU.”

Ali Vaez, Iran project director for the International Crisis Group, compared the strait to a “sword of Damocles over Trump.”

“Iran wants to front-load benefits without surrendering its main leverage, which is Hormuz,” Mr. Vaez said.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump told Axios that he believes that Iran will eventually come around because of economic distress and inflation. He did not threaten new military action against Iran, saying, “We are low-keying it.”

Iran’s demands were listed on Saturday by Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. He called for the United States to lift its naval blockade and sanctions on Iran’s oil and petrochemical exports, withdraw the U. S. military from around Iran, pay war reparations and release frozen Iranian assets, as well as end attacks on Iran’s allies in the region, including in Lebanon, and threats against the country.

All those demands, except for reparations, are spelled out in the 14-point June memorandum. Most of the agreement’s terms were violated within weeks, with even Mr. Trump declaring the deal “over.”

The demand for reparations is also a familiar one, and Iranian officials have said in local media that the issue is a bargaining chip to get as much sanctions relief from Washington as possible, Mr. Vaez said.

Iran’s negotiations with Oman on how traffic would move through the strait once it is open are essentially done, Mr. Vaez said. But Iran wants to tie the strait to the restoration of the memorandum, which would require further talks with the United States, he said. Any talks on the future of Iran’s nuclear program, which is one of the main reasons Mr. Trump said he began this war, are dependent on a restoration of the memorandum.

On Sunday, speaking to journalists, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi of Iran said, “Talks with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz are progressing well and in final stages as experts are working on maps.”

He continued, “However, an agreement with Oman does not mean reopening the strait, which remains dependent on fulfilling conditions conveyed through mediators.”

Part of the confusion stems from divisions within the Iranian system about how to proceed, which has led to the emphasizing of these demands, said Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa program at Chatham House, the London think tank.

Some officials see diplomacy as the best path to economic reconstruction, she said. While others, the hard-liners, “are so skeptical and paranoid that they would prefer to hold on to their leverage rather than think of the economy,” gambling that Mr. Trump will not resume the war.

But the Iranians also see Washington as divided, she said, with some officials pushing for diplomacy and others for more bombing, and Mr. Trump “blowing one way or another.” There are also those in Washington who believe that once the strait is open, Mr. Trump would be tempted to walk away from the whole issue and leave Iran’s highly enriched uranium buried in the ground.

The Iranians “don’t want to do this for free,” Ms. Vakil said. “The strait is not about fees, it’s about control and leverage for the rest of the package.”

And it is about trust, Mr. Batmanghelidj said. Iran could have made more extreme demands, he said, but has chosen to try to return to the memorandum as the basis for a permanent end to the war. “What matters less is the particular figure or amount or concession, but what the U. S. can do to prove to Iran that it can make good on any of these commitments.”

The memorandum of understanding “is the floor from which everyone will try to build a structure for a deal,” Ms. Vakil said. “But we’re far away from that.”

Steven Erlanger is the chief diplomatic correspondent in Europe and is based in Berlin. He has reported from over 120 countries, including Thailand, France, Israel, Germany and the former Soviet Union.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Ken Kesey’s psychedelic bus, immortalized in “The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test,” is preparing for one more run. And to its owners, America sure could use it.

Credit...

Supported by

By Heather Knight

Visuals by Ricardo Nagaoka

Reporting from Pleasant Hill, Ore.

Among the rolling hills outside Eugene, Ore., down a winding gravel path and inside a big barn sits a school bus built in 1939. Its once-blazing colors have faded. Its roof is crumbling. Its windows are cracked. The only regular occupants these days are insects.

It might look like a hunk of junk, but the muted technicolor splotches tell the story of one of the most exuberant periods of San Francisco history.

Sixty years ago, this bus symbolized the city’s counterculture revolution, the embrace of psychedelic drugs and the live-out-loud, love-your-neighbor ethos for which the era is remembered.

With the nation once again facing war, polarized politics and cultural battles, Zane Kesey thinks some of that old bus magic is needed. And that is why he has agreed to send the bus, the one he helped cover in swirls of Day-Glo paint when he was 3, back to the city that spawned a movement.

“I would love to see it adored again,” he said. “And for people to feel that pure, innocent love that came out of it.”

His father, Ken Kesey, who died in 2001, had just written the novel “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest” when he purchased the former school bus that a large Bay Area family had tricked out with beds, benches and a refrigerator for road trips. Mr. Kesey and his freethinking friends, called the Merry Pranksters, painted the bus in psychedelic colors, cut a sun roof into it, added a powerful sound system and installed a balcony on top.

A sign on the back read, “Caution: Weird Load.” Above the windshield, where a bus typically displays its destination, somebody painted the misspelled word, “Furthur.” And the name for the bus stuck.

The pranksters set out on a cross-country trip, smoking weed, tripping on LSD and spreading the gospel of opening your mind, man.

The journey was documented in Tom Wolfe’s 1968 book, “The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test,” hailed by The New York Times back then as not only “the best book on the hippies,” but also “essential.” The bus and its beatnik driver, Neal Cassady, appeared in the Grateful Dead song “The Other One,” which references “Cowboy Neal at the wheel of the bus to never-ever land.”

The bus became part of the landscape of San Francisco’s counterculture movement. In 1967, Mr. Kesey drove it into Golden Gate Park for the Human Be-In, a gathering to protest a California law banning LSD. The event was a precursor to the city’s Summer of Love later that year, during which tens of thousands of young, idealistic people poured into the city’s Haight-Ashbury neighborhood and the park to protest the Vietnam War and promote hallucinogenic drugs and free love.

Those days are long gone, and San Francisco is now known more for A. I. than LSD, more for billionaires than beatniks. But Zane Kesey aims to bring some of that old flavor back — with his dad’s bus.

So later this month, it will leave the Kesey family farm in Pleasant Hill, Ore., a short drive from Eugene, for the first time since 1969. A flatbed truck will carry it down Interstate 5 to California, over the Bay Bridge and into the city. In the dead of night, when the streets are quiet, it will trundle into Golden Gate Park and into its Hall of Flowers alongside the botanical gardens.

There, starting Sept. 5, the bus will be on display as part of a show called “Forever Grateful, Golden Gate Park,” put on by the Haight Street Art Center, which aims to preserve and showcase art and cultural artifacts from the city’s counterculture movement. The exhibit will also feature Jerry Garcia’s BMW, live performers, puppetry and storytelling.

Kelly Harris, the center’s executive director, visited the farm and said that while the bus looked like a relic now, it still exuded an energy that was “magical and connective.”

Roger McNamee, the chairman of the center’s board, called the bus “the Rosetta stone of San Francisco’s counterculture” and said he hoped that those who view it, including young people who have never heard of it, see parallels to today.

“There is this expectation that we will live in a world dominated by technology, dominated by capital, where everyone is expected to play their role and have very little control over their own futures,” he said in an interview, noting Mr. Kesey and his pranksters had decided not to conform and instead forged their own wild, joyful path.

“If everybody went and sat with this bus for a bit and thought about what it meant, I think they’d be happier,” Mr. McNamee said.

Zane Kesey, 65, sure hopes so. He is the kind of man who offers hugs to strangers, wears tie-dyed shirts and talks about the bus as if it were a person with feelings.

“She’s happy, you can tell,” he said, noting that the crescent-moon-shaped silver bumper, which was restored to its front for the journey to California, resembles a smile. “She’s thrilled to have people talking about her, paying attention to her and all that she meant.”

He has never known life without the bus, he said. He remembers getting blue paint in his hair when the pranksters decorated it. And he recalls riding on its balcony as Mr. Cassady practiced driving it, tearing around the bends a bit too fast.

“Dad was a magician, and the bus was just one of his tools,” Mr. Kesey said. “I didn’t know it was unusual. If you grow up in the circus, the circus is all you know.”

His father grew up in Oregon and moved to the Bay Area for a graduate writing program at Stanford University. As the 1960s wound down, he returned to his family farm to write, teach and raise his four children, and the bus has remained there ever since.

Zane Kesey gave a tour of the farm, including the small cemetery where his father and brother, Jed, are buried. Jed Kesey died at age 20 after a van carrying the University of Oregon wrestling team plunged off a cliff. Ken Kesey died at age 66.

Beyond the cemetery, past a thicket of trees and a now-dry creek bed, is the spot where the bus sat for many years, hidden from view with blackberry vines growing over it, before it was moved into the barn for protection.

According to Stephanie Kesey, Zane Kesey’s wife, the news anchor Walter Cronkite once came to the farm to film a story about the bus, and his cameraman plunged through a rickety wooden bridge and into the creek.

Officials with the Smithsonian have also visited, wanting the bus but leaving instead with a plywood sign that the Merry Pranksters used as a makeshift bulletin board on their bus trip and that was found covered in feathers in a chicken coop.

“A family of foxes occupied the rear seat of Furthur, moldering in a field, so Kesey decided to donate this sign instead of the bus,” reads the museum’s website.

Stephanie Kesey said the idea after the exhibit ends in late October is to store the bus in a Burning Man warehouse in the East Bay while a fund-raising campaign proceeds to restore it and permanently display it in San Francisco.

“I don’t think we’ll ever see it come back to the farm,” she said, adding that it was important for the public to view it again.

“Our need for color right now is very real,” she said. “And peace and love, exploration and kindness.”

Zane Kesey said his father would be a little sad that the bus is leaving the farm but thrilled that it is returning to San Francisco.

“You know San Francisco,” he said. “You leave your heart there.”

Stephanie Kesey grew a little misty and nodded.

“I think it’s going home,” she said.

San Francisco's counterculture movement was before my time, but I've heard a lot about it having lived in the city for 27 years. I was thrilled to take a deep dive into the era for this story, reading "The Electric Kool-Aid Acid Test" and visiting the Kesey farm in Oregon. While San Francisco has changed a lot, I'm so glad its whimsical spirit and embrace of quirkiness continues.

Heather Knight is a reporter in San Francisco, leading The Times’s coverage of the Bay Area and Northern California.

How a Drone ‘Hellscape’ Might Stop a Chinese Invasion of Taiwan

The New York Times August 09, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Inspired by Ukraine’s battlefield gains, Taiwan is betting on drones to deter a potential Chinese invasion.

By Chris Buckley and Amy Chang Chien

Reporting from Taipei, Taiwan

To repel any future Chinese invasion, Taiwan is building fleets of flying drones and unmanned attack boats.

The goal is to use them to help locate and attack Chinese forces approaching the island, relying on Taiwanese soldiers trained to move quickly before China can strike them. U. S. commanders who developed this strategy call it a “hellscape”: overwhelming an invading force with waves of drones, missiles and artillery, and making an amphibious assault so risky that China’s leaders are deterred from trying.

Inspired by lessons from Ukraine and other recent war zones, Taiwan is now accelerating efforts to put that strategy into practice.

“Our drone and counter-drone efforts started relatively late, and initially we were trying things out as we went along,” Lt. Gen. Huang Wen-chi, the director general of strategic planning for the Taiwanese Defense Ministry, told a committee of lawmakers on Wednesday. That has begun to change over the past two years, he added.

On Thursday, Taiwan’s military allowed reporters to watch as troops in central Taiwan practiced using drones for reconnaissance, as part of the island’s annual Han Kuang military exercises, which began on Wednesday and will run for 10 days.

Maj. Gen. Lu Wen-yuan, who helped plan the exercises, said earlier that they would also train troops to take out enemy drones.

Many militaries across the world are embracing the drone revolution, but Taiwan faces a particularly urgent threat: China, which is roughly 110 miles away, claims the self-governed island as its territory. Chinese leaders say they want to absorb Taiwan peacefully but will not rule out using force. They are backing that threat with expanding fleets of warships, planes, missiles and drones, as well as more frequent coast guard patrols and landing exercises.

Taiwanese officials have noted Ukraine’s drone-driven gains on the battlefield, and they are trying to emulate Ukraine’s David-versus-Goliath approach: using relatively cheap and nimble drones to level the playing field against a much larger adversary.

“Drones are entering a new chapter,” said Max Lo, the chairman of the Taiwan National Drone Industry Association. “Taiwan, for its own survival and national defense, is in urgent need of these drones. But it’s the same everywhere in the world right now — that’s an opportunity for Taiwan.”

Aiming to make the island a drone industry superpower, the government says it wants Taiwan to make 100,000 drones a month by 2030, with around half exported. It also wants the military to acquire over 210,000 flying and seaborne drones.

Taiwan has “realized that drones will be important in all the domains, in all the phases,” in a potential war with China, said Mick Ryan, a retired Australian major general who has studied Ukraine and Taiwan.

Ukraine’s recent success at longer-range drone strikes suggests that Taiwan could also attack ships leaving Chinese ports if Beijing launched an amphibious assault, said Mr. Ryan, now a senior fellow at the Lowy Institute in Sydney.

China’s army is not yet strong enough to easily invade Taiwan, many experts believe, and recent purges in the People’s Liberation Army’s high command have undermined its readiness. But like Taiwan’s military, it has been building up fleets of crewless planes and boats, and is investing heavily in technology to detect and jam drones.

“Remember, the Chinese are also watching everything the Ukrainians are doing,” Mr. Ryan added.

For Taiwan, acquiring the drones may be the straightforward part. To master drone warfare, Taiwan must also retool its military organization, training and doctrine. It must learn to operate swarms of drones, rapidly assess and share the intelligence they provide and prevent an enemy from disabling them, according to experts. This will require troops to be more mobile and self-sustaining.

“The army’s frontline military operations must undergo a total change from the past,” said Shu Hsiao-Huang, an associate research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research in Taipei, which is supported by Taiwan’s Defense Ministry. “In the Russia-Ukraine War, if you fire one round, you won’t have a chance to fire a second, if you just stay lined up there without moving on,” he said.

Unlike Ukraine, though, Taiwan lacks the pressure of an actual invasion to mobilize resources and force changes. “It’s very difficult, because they haven’t experienced the crucible of war,” Mr. Shu said.

But military units have been working to learn drone tactics, which are a focus of the continuing Han Kuang exercises.

The Taiwanese army also released pictures from a drill last month in which a unit scrambled to defend islands off Taiwan’s east coast by using drones to hunt for enemy forces. On Saturday, Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, watched an exercise in the island’s south where troops tested two types of prototype drones designed to strike invading forces.

Taiwan also recently created a Littoral Combat Command, integrating drones, mobile missiles and artillery into a coastal shield against potential Chinese invasion.

Still, Taiwan is a long way from meeting the complex demands of 21st-century warfare, many experts said. It risks becoming “focused on the technology more than the equally essential organizational and doctrinal changes that are needed to implement a hellscape concept,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security and an author of a recent study of Taiwan’s drone warfare strategy.

In the event of an invasion, China is likely to try to seal off Taiwan from external support. To survive a blockade, Taiwan needs to build stockpiles and expand homegrown drone production, especially “cheaper, shorter-range one-way attack drones,” Ms. Pettyjohn said.

Both sides of Taiwan’s polarized political landscape agree on building more drones, even if they disagree on the details. Taiwan’s government has proposed spending $6.5 billion over five years to buy drones. But two opposition parties that hold the majority in its legislature rejected the plan, arguing that it could attract graft and create waste. The main opposition Nationalist Party has proposed spending $7.4 billion over six years, with requirements for growing levels of domestic production.

As lawmakers debate spending, Taiwanese and U. S. drone makers are competing for potential orders.

Thunder Tiger, a Taiwanese manufacturer, and Shield AI, an American defense technology company, last month staged a trial run for two models of sea drones that could scout for enemy vessels and blow them up. But Chen Kwan-ju, the chairman of Thunder Tiger, said the company is seeking more policy certainty before it expands production partnerships.

At the same time, Taiwan is rapidly increasing its rate of drone exports, seeking to make itself an indispensable supplier of components for other democratic states that want to reduce their reliance on Chinese parts, which raise concerns about supply disruptions, or espionage.

In the first three months of 2026, Taiwan exported drones worth $115 million, exceeding its total drone exports for all of 2025, according to the island’s Ministry of Economic Affairs. The top destination is the Czech Republic, though many of the drones find their way to nearby Ukraine, research shows.

Taiwan’s exports of drone components are probably even higher. Demand for these parts, such as motors and optical equipment, is likely to grow, according to representatives of U. S. drone companies.

“Taiwan sits at the center of one of the most important industrial and strategic competitions of our time,” Michael Robbins, the president of the Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International, wrote in an email. “It is one of the few places positioned to produce trusted drone components at scale.”

Chris Buckley, the chief China correspondent for The Times, reports on China and Taiwan from Taipei, focused on politics, social change and security and military issues.

Amy Chang Chien is a reporter and researcher for The Times in Taipei, covering Taiwan and China.

Please Judge the Books I’m Reading

The New York Times August 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Radhika Jones

Ms. Jones, a former editor in chief of Vanity Fair, is at work on a memoir, “Bookish.”

I was well into adulthood before I learned that prestigious cultural awards are distributed not by some array of gods and muses but by real people. So when the Booker Prize Foundation released its longlist almost two weeks ago, I read it with pleasure, and I was struck by how prominently the award’s five judges featured in the announcement. There they are, most of them smiling beatifically in the photo on the Booker website and cradling two stacks of books, the proud result of months of curatorial labor and, presumably, high-minded sparring and arm-twisting.

Literary judges often take the brunt of critiques about prize giving in the arts, what with their inherent biases, their inescapable blind spots and the cliquish nature of the process by which they anoint winners. It’s easy to snipe at their qualifications and choices. Judges are the ultimate gatekeepers, a 21st-century taboo personified. But at a moment when chatbot guidance is intruding into every endeavor, I was glad to see these living, breathing humans pictured along with their selections. The subjectivity is the point.

I’ve adjudicated several awards and prizes through the years, and the dynamics around a judging table — the wild range of reactions to prose style, the tactics of persuasion, the parsing of emotional impact — are as human as the work in front of us. It’s not unusual for a judge to bang a fist on the table and storm out of a room (or, during those wretched Covid years, exit the Zoom). It’s also possible to incept a notion and change another judge’s mind. Some judging panels enjoy consensus from the outset, but it’s more common to navigate through conflict. Often where we landed wasn’t where we thought we were headed, which was part of the fun.

In a world where, apparently, fewer people read anything, those of us who still read a lot rely on literary prizes to assist with short-term discovery and long-term predictive power. Prizes are the original recommendation engine — except the deciders are tasked with consulting their own taste, not some algorithmic projection.

This year’s judging chair for the Booker Prize is the classicist Mary Beard, perfectly cast as an authority figure during a summer when all anyone wants to talk about is “The Odyssey.” Her fellow judges include the poet Raymond Antrobus, the musician Jarvis Cocker, the poet and memoirist Patricia Lockwood and the editor and critic Rebecca Liu. I don’t know any of them personally. I don’t yet know the Venn diagram between my sensibility and theirs, and I haven’t yet read any of the novels on the longlist, but I am happier than ever to take a flyer and find out.

Modern prize culture has existed for about 125 years; James F. English, in his excellent book “The Economy of Prestige,” dates the current craze for literary awards to the Nobel Prize, which debuted in 1901. In the Anglophone world, that timing happens to coincide roughly with the rise of English literature departments and, together, universities and awards like the Pulitzer, the National Book Awards and the Booker have become engines of canonization.

Universities canonize works by adopting them into curriculums, ensuring that generations of students will read them. (Scholars who assemble anthologies often do this work literally, binding poems, plays, fiction and essays into textbook editions.) Prizes canonize works and authors by setting them above their contemporaries, increasing the chances that when the literary detritus of the present is washed away, a few standouts will remain.

Since we can’t read all the books all the time, it’s helpful to have some guidance, however flawed, as to what’s most worthy of our sustained attention. That’s where prizes come in. Awards possess the power to attract immediate attention, both from their selections and from their scandals. (Nearly seven years ago the Booker caused a furor by shirking its bylaws and shruggingly handing out a tie.) But they also hold institutional sway.

Prizes have become especially important if you believe that our society has reached a postliterate stage, in which fewer students are majoring in English literature and almost no one in college can read full books anymore. If academic canons calcify and special interest groups continue to target works deemed controversial or unaligned with their worldviews, it will become harder for new books to be anointed through an educational pipeline. The recently published K-12 required-reading syllabus for Texas public schools, which in its high school years includes no books published in the past half-century, offers a glimpse of what that looks like.

I don’t mean to say readers shouldn’t abide by the suggestions of their trusted critic or columnist, family bibliophile, Substacker or BookToker. As a society, we do not lack for individual opinions about books, and many of those opinions are reliable. So by all means, take recommendations from me and Dua Lipa.

But I put extra store in prizes’ ability to affect and encourage collective reading because so much of their value, albeit unseen, comes from the collective act of judging — discussing, debating, deciding — and the subsequent broadcasting and coverage of those choices. When effort is made to put together a group of judges with diverse backgrounds and artistic experience, it shows in the output.

This year’s Booker Prize committee is admirably idiosyncratic, and so is the longlist it selected. I’ve had a soft spot for the Booker since the halcyon late 1980s and early ’90s wins for Kazuo Ishiguro, A. S. Byatt, Peter Carey and J. M. Coetzee. More recently, last year’s longlist led me and my book club to “Seascraper,” a small but mighty novel by Benjamin Wood about the hopes and dreams of an English shrimp catcher. I am 100 percent certain I would not have bought that book had it not been cited by the Booker judges, and I’m as grateful to them as if they had given it to me directly.

Imagine if the Television Academy ditched its broad-based secret balloting and instead just invited Mike White, Shonda Rhimes, Taylor Sheridan, Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Bowen Yang into a room to duke it out over best drama. I would absolutely watch whatever winning show they told me to watch — the quirkier, the better.

As the trend lines for reading descend — and time spent scrolling, viewing, favoriting and following goes up — I take heart in the willingness of individuals to keep seeking the magical connection that imaginative literature can provide. Sometimes the connection is private, and sometimes it’s shared with other readers, but either way, it’s inherently personal. Awards, with their rare power to grant credibility in a cacophonous world and their equal capacity to provoke conversation, remind us that subjectivity is part of the risk and value of consuming art.

Maybe 50 years from now, no one will read literary fiction anymore, and nearly 200 years of canonizing energy — the effort to whittle down our mad surfeit of books into a working library that is, if not manageable, then at least comprehensible — will have been spent in vain. But if anybody still wants to pick up a novel after the deluge, I predict these Booker longlists and shortlists, along with those of the Pulitzers, the National Book Awards and other prizes subject to human whim and discretion, will provide essential signposts.

Like the books they recognize, these lists convey something crucial about the imperfect, unpredictable world we live in. They’ll be evidence of the brief, shining period when a handful of creative people would — by choice! — spend the better part of a year buried in books, deploying their time and taste in support of the ones they hoped other people would read.

Radhika Jones is a former editor in chief of Vanity Fair and previously served as the editorial director of books at The Times. She is at work on a memoir, “Bookish,” and writes a newsletter on literature and culture.

Michigan Senate Candidate, a Former Trump Critic, Shifts Toward Election Skepticism

The New York Times August 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee, has suggested that further scrutiny of the 2020 election was warranted and that voting irregularities sank his first Senate bid two years ago.

By Beth Reinhard

In the chaotic aftermath of the 2020 election, as President Trump refused to accept defeat and pumped out false claims about voter fraud, Mike Rogers was a clear and consistent voice of reproach.

Mr. Rogers, a former Republican representative from Michigan, denounced Mr. Trump’s efforts to undermine the election as “cause for both concern and alarm.” He ripped the president’s pressure on Georgia’s top election official “as more gangster than presidential.” As for Mr. Trump’s role in the riot at the U. S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, Mr. Rogers declared, “You’re damn right you had responsibility for this.”

But as he aims to return to Washington, in a Senate race considered key to control of that chamber, Mr. Rogers has become an election skeptic. Minutes after the president’s recent speech filled with outlandish accusations about voting fraud — including a debunked claim about Michigan ballots — Mr. Rogers weighed in, suggesting that further scrutiny of the election was warranted.

“I am thankful for President Trump’s commitment to transparency,” Mr. Rogers said on his social media accounts. “The news coming out of the White House tonight is deeply troubling — especially that of a voter fraud scheme right here in Michigan.”

Mr. Rogers has also suggested that voting irregularities sank his Senate bid two years ago — based on an unproven claim about late-arriving Detroit ballots that Mr. Trump has amplified and that echoed accusations made by election deniers in 2020.

Mr. Rogers’s pivot on voting issues reflects the journey of a politician who built a national reputation as a mainstream Republican more than a decade ago, in the pre-Trump era, and is attempting a second act in a political arena remade by a president who demands absolute fealty from his fellow Republicans.

“Now he’s toeing the MAGA line,” said former Representative Fred Upton, a Michigan Republican who served with Mr. Rogers in the House and calls him a friend. “I don’t want to speculate on his motives for talking about the 2020 election, but that election is over. The 2024 election is over.”

In response to questions from The New York Times about Mr. Rogers’s recent comments about the 2020 election and his loss in 2024, Alyssa Brouillet, the campaign spokeswoman, blamed Democrats for undermining public faith in elections.

“This is about protecting free and fair elections,” she said. “Every American deserves to know that their vote counts and isn’t canceled out by an illegal vote.”

Mr. Rogers’s campaign did not provide any evidence to back up his claim about his 2024 defeat.

Mr. Rogers now faces the newly minted Democratic nominee, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official from the left wing of his party, in the November election. Mr. Trump said earlier this week that Dr. El-Sayed had “a real shot” in a state he claimed was riddled with voter fraud.

“Get ready for another Rigged Election,” he said.

Mr. Rogers, 63, is a former F. B. I. special agent and Army officer who served in Congress for 14 years, including four as the powerful chairman of the House Intelligence Committee. One of his party’s leading voices on national security and foreign policy, Mr. Rogers was a frequent guest on Sunday morning talk shows. When he announced he would not seek re-election in 2014, a Democratic colleague described him as “a voice for moderation and consensus-building.”

Mr. Rogers was working as a CNN commentator in 2020 when Mr. Trump rejected Joe Biden’s victory and argued the election had been rigged.

“I think it’s very corrosive,” Mr. Rogers said in one of several cable network appearances criticizing the president. Mr. Rogers also wrote columns in The Detroit News and The Washington Post that accused Mr. Trump of setting “an exceptionally dangerous precedent” and of making claims “without proof, only conspiracy and hearsay.”

In 2022, as Mr. Rogers explored a possible presidential bid by visiting early-voting primary states, he called the president’s tactics “clearly destructive” and said, “Trump’s time has passed.”

But Mr. Rogers’s political calculus appeared to change the next year, when he decided to run for an open Senate seat. He joined a crowded Republican field and landed Mr. Trump’s endorsement. Mr. Trump viewed the former congressman as the strongest Senate candidate in a state key to his re-election, and the two men built a rapport during the 2024 campaign, according to a person familiar with the relationship who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The editorial board of The Detroit Free Press reported in June 2024 that when it asked the Senate candidate whether Mr. Biden won the 2020 election, he refused to answer — a sign of Mr. Rogers’s newfound loyalty to Mr. Trump.

Mr. Rogers won the primary two months later but narrowly lost to Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, even as Mr. Trump carried the state. Weeks later, an aide to the president-elect quashed speculation that Mr. Rogers was under consideration for F. B. I. director amid a backlash from MAGA influencers, who saw the former intelligence official who had worked for CNN as part of the loathed “deep state.”

But after Senator Gary Peters, a Michigan Democrat, announced his retirement in January 2025, Mr. Rogers said Mr. Trump convinced him to get back on the campaign trail.

“The president called and said, ‘Mike, I need you to do this. I need you in the Senate, and here’s the only thing I’m going to ask you: win,’ ” Mr. Rogers told a Republican group in Muskegon, Mich., in October 2025, according to video reviewed by The Times.

At that same event, Mr. Rogers cast doubt on the legitimacy of Ms. Slotkin’s victory, referring to a van carrying ballots that “showed up” in Detroit the morning after the election. He gave the same account at another event earlier that month and said those ballots had “swung the election.” His comments about the van were previously reported by The Detroit News.

“Mike Rogers knows better,” said Christopher Thomas, who served as Michigan’s elections director for more than three decades before becoming an adviser to voting officials in Detroit. “Mike Rogers knows no one stole the election from him in 2024, and he knows full well no one stole the election from Trump in 2020.”

This year, Mr. Rogers is running not just with the president’s endorsement but also with the help of many of his closest associates. His current campaign team includes Chris LaCivita, a co-manager of Mr. Trump’s 2024 campaign; Katie Walsh Shields, Mr. Trump’s former deputy chief of staff; and Tony Fabrizio, a pollster and senior adviser to the president.

Norm Shinkle, a veteran Republican Party leader in Michigan, dismissed the former congressman’s past criticism of the president.

“If you took all the Republicans who used to be critical of Trump and disqualified them, the president would lose half his cabinet,” Mr. Shinkle quipped. “I think if Mike Rogers thought Trump did something wrong he might correct him again, but now that he’s got his endorsement he might do it more politely.”

Linda Lee Tarver, a Republican activist in Michigan who backed Mr. Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election, said she did not blame Mr. Rogers for opposing those efforts six years ago. “He didn’t have all the information,” she said. Ms. Tarver also suggested that Mr. Rogers’s view of that vote might have changed after his loss in the 2024 Senate race.

“We know in our hearts that he won,” said Ms. Tarver, who is serving on Mr. Rogers’s campaign coalition of religious leaders. “Tell me, how would you feel about losing by 19,000 votes in a state with illegal voting? That had to have changed his view.”

Cheri Hardmon, spokeswoman for the Michigan Secretary of State, said Mr. Rogers never formally raised concerns about the election results by requesting a recount or filing a court challenge. She described elections in the state as “safe, secure.”

Mr. Upton, the former Michigan representative, predicted that Mr. Rogers would now lean toward the political center in an effort to court the independent and moderate voters who are key to winning a Midwestern swing state.

Only 33 percent of likely Michigan voters say the president is doing an excellent or pretty good job, according to a recent Epic-MRA poll. “You’ll see the old Mike Rogers,” Mr. Upton said.

On Friday, Mr. Rogers posted a video to his social media accounts speaking directly to Democrats about housing, education and taxes. “You have a home with us,” he said.

But Mr. Trump remains fixated on voting fraud and has seized on Mr. Rogers’s claim about his defeat in the 2024 Senate race. In a speech to the Detroit Economic Club in January, the president asserted Mr. Rogers “won” a Senate seat two years ago and said, “I think they took that away from you last time.”

“They rigged the election on you,” he added.

Mr. Rogers posted the president’s remarks on X and featured them in a fund-raising appeal.

When the two men campaigned together last month in Michigan, Mr. Trump said, “I happen to think he won last time.”

Mr. Rogers vowed that if he were elected to the Senate, he would help pass legislation backed by the president that would impose nationwide voter identification and proof of citizenship requirements and limit voting by mail.

Mr. Trump then called up John James, a Republican candidate for governor, to the stage. “Thank you Mr. President for coming back to Michigan, where you’ve won three times,” Mr. James said. (Mr. Trump carried the state in 2016 and 2024 but lost in 2020.)

Mr. Rogers stood to Mr. James’s right, his hands clasped.

Beth Reinhard is an investigative reporter for The Times covering politics.
