The curious case of Guren “Bobby” Zhou shows the ease with which investors with shady backgrounds and unknown motivations can funnel money to the president.

Guren “Bobby” Zhou, top left, with Zach Witkoff, right, in a private suite at the World Cup final match on July 19 in East Rutherford, N. J. Credit... Vincent Alban for The New York Times

Supported by

By Russ Buettner

Russ Buettner covers the Trump family’s finances.

During the World Cup soccer final in New Jersey last month, Zach Witkoff, co-founder of President Trump’s cryptocurrency company, took in the action from a luxury suite. Joining him was a man who had made the president, and all the company’s co-founders, much richer.

Two years earlier, the man, Guren “Bobby” Zhou, was a failed hardwood flooring retailer in Britain who had come under investigation there for money laundering and presided over the collapse of a small crypto start-up.

Then seemingly out of nowhere, he became one of the biggest buyers of tokens from Mr. Trump’s company, World Liberty Financial, dropping a total of $100 million through a new firm called Aqua 1. He kept quiet about it for months, other than speaking briefly as “Mr. Bobby” from Aqua 1 during a little-noticed audio stream on X.

“We’re very proud to be a major player in the World Liberty, which is Trump’s family’s crypto venture,” he said.

Under World Liberty policy, as much as $75 million of that money was distributed to a company controlled by the president and his three sons. The money also benefited the family of Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s special peace envoy and the father of Zach Witkoff.

In any prior era, a windfall for the president of that size from a foreigner with no public signs of access to that level of wealth would have certainly gone against norms and might have spawned a congressional investigation.

Instead, the curious case of Mr. Zhou illustrates the ease with which buyers with unknown backgrounds and motivations can use the anonymity of cryptocurrency to shower Mr. Trump with money. The president’s recent financial disclosure form shows that he collected $1.4 billion from his crypto businesses last year, the majority of it from anonymous sources.

It is not clear how closely World Liberty scrutinized Mr. Zhou’s past, but the money laundering investigation in England was publicly available information, as were portions of Mr. Zhou’s troubled business history.

A court record filed last November accuses Mr. Zhou of participating with five other people in a money laundering effort beginning in 2019. Mr. Zhou has not been charged. British officials said late last month that their investigation remained active.

His transaction with World Liberty raises questions as to how he was able to access so much money, and how fully the company followed anti-money laundering laws. Such laws require businesses, in certain situations, to document the source of their customers’ funds before accepting the money.

Patrick Prinz, the chief operating officer of Recoveris, a Switzerland-based firm that investigates digital asset crimes, said a combination of the red flags described to him by The New York Times should have triggered the documentation requirement: Mr. Zhou’s business failures, his sudden access to wealth, the size of the transaction and the investigation.

David Wachsman, a spokesman for World Liberty, said in a statement that the company had followed all applicable laws and regulations. “World Liberty maintains a compliance program that meets or exceeds industry standards,” he said.

Mr. Wachsman declined to say whether the company was aware of the source of the funds used in the purchase. He said the company disputed The Times’s “characterization of Mr. Zhou,” but did not cite any specifics.

A White House spokeswoman, Anna Kelly, said Mr. Trump had no conflicts of interest and “only acts in the best interests of the American public.”

Mr. Zhou did not respond to numerous messages to him and his company. Reuters first identified Mr. Zhou as the person behind Aqua 1.

Even now the source of the money that Mr. Zhou paid to World Liberty remains a mystery.

But a deep examination of his career by The Times — through dozens of interviews with former associates, reviews of confidential documents and an analysis of court records and other publicly available information — shows a curious arc. A man who seemed to be constantly asking for money from others had a significant change in fortune just after his crypto company burned through $7.6 million and he decamped from London to the United Arab Emirates in the summer of 2024.

Many former associates would speak only on the condition of anonymity because they feared being pulled into the investigation in England or worried about the risk of violating libel laws in the Emirates that make defamation a potential crime, even if true.

They describe Mr. Zhou as a high-octane charmer with a British accent, persuasive enough to sell ice in a snowstorm, as one said. But all were stunned to learn that after his departure from London, he was able to purchase $100 million in anything.

Several business professionals told The Times that they had refused to get involved with Mr. Zhou after researching his background. World Liberty, on the other hand, welcomed his company with open arms.

“We’re excited to work hand-in-hand with the team at Aqua 1,” said Zak Folkman, a co-founder of World Liberty Financial, in a statement on X.

For most of his adult life, Mr. Zhou worked far from technology and high finance.

Raised in Shanghai, he moved to England in 2005 to attend graduate school. While living in student housing at the University of Lancashire, he launched a business to distribute hardwood flooring that his father milled back home.

He eventually took over a flooring factory in Italy, a small website and a chain of 20 retail stores. A photograph in a local newspaper of one store showed a small, corrugated steel structure with bright green signs declaring “YOU SAVE MORE.”

In 2017, he heard that economic development officials from Wales would be visiting Shanghai on a trade mission and arranged a meeting. Mr. Zhou, then 32, told the group that he planned to open a flooring store within 25 miles of every Welsh resident.

“That struck me as perhaps overly ambitious and not really reflecting the way that Welsh life really works, in that we are quite a rural country,” said Ken Skates, then the minister of economic development for Wales.

Mr. Zhou’s plan would not come about. A year after the meeting, he placed his companies in administration, the British equivalent of bankruptcy restructuring. He sold the stores during that process at no gain, without repaying the $5 million that his books showed he owed his father’s company, according to court records.

An associate recalled Mr. Zhou saying, before his company collapsed, that he would be receiving $10 million from a Chinese company. The money did not arrive, and the associate came to doubt the commitment was ever real.

But Mr. Zhou’s partner in the Italian factory, an American named Thomas Corey Lewis, still believes Mr. Zhou had important connections in China and extraordinary powers of persuasion.

“He had the intellectual capacity to sit down and convince a board of smart people to fund him,” Mr. Lewis said recently.

About that time, Mr. Zhou lived in a modest 1,200-square-foot flat in Southampton, roughly a two-hour drive from London, records show. His wife and their young daughter had joined him from Shanghai. He played table tennis in a recreational league.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, Mr. Zhou imported masks and tests from China, generating some income.

In 2020, he told one local newspaper that he was a partner in a boutique investment firm and a managing director of a financial institution called Valens Bank.

Records show that the investment firm had one unidentified employee, with assets of less than $1 million, and went dormant two years later. Valens, a small institution based in Frankfurt, told The Times in an emailed statement that Mr. Zhou never held a position with the company but had been a minority shareholder.

Mr. Zhou also launched a family office, a form of lightly regulated firm that handles investments, and in some cases personal affairs, of wealthy families. The office drew just one client, a recent immigrant from Singapore named Ander Tsui. Mr. Zhou told associates that Mr. Tsui had made significant money as an early crypto investor.

Mr. Tsui, who did not communicate in English, relied on Mr. Zhou to help him navigate life in London, former associates said.

The two began working together on a company they called Caduceus, with the goal of seizing on the latest craze in crypto.

At a posh London nightclub in late 2021, Mr. Zhou danced in front of his investors and employees, waving a sign that read “Caduceus Xmas Party.” Servers chanted at him as they thrust champagne bottles strapped with sparklers above their heads.

That came after dinner at a high-end Chinese restaurant and lunch at a private social club.

“Absolutely unreal,” one attendee wrote on Facebook with videos from the day.

The splashy affair, and others like it, were part of Mr. Zhou’s marketing efforts to sell digital tokens to fund the Caduceus product: a tool for creating virtual “metaverses” where humans interact as avatars.

To lure investors, Mr. Zhou issued a string of announcements claiming the support of well-financed companies.

In February 2022, he took a group to the BRIT Awards, Britain’s biggest ceremony for popular music. Caduceus cosponsored an after-party on the Dixie Queen, a replica of a 19th-century paddle steamer that cruises the Thames. Mr. Zhou invited acquaintances, including an executive of China Merchant Securities (UK), the London subsidiary of a state-owned financial services firm in China.

The following morning, Mr. Zhou issued a news release announcing that China Merchant Securities (UK) would form a $1 billion venture fund for projects based on Caduceus technology.

China Merchant Securities (UK) demanded that Mr. Zhou’s companies stop using its name, according to an email reviewed by The Times. But Mr. Zhou persisted.

Michael Butler, head of compliance for China Merchants Securities (UK), told The Times in an email that the company was not involved in any such fund or in Caduceus. “The use of the firm’s name, and the listing of an individual as connected to the project, were unauthorized and materially false,” he wrote.

On April 1, 2022, Mr. Zhou’s Caduceus announced another major supporter: the Bin Zayed Group, which was founded by Sheikh Khaled Zayed Saquer Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family. The announcement called the Bin Zayed Group a “lead investor” in a $4 million round of funding.

Caduceus marketing materials from that spring obtained by The Times listed Midhat Kidwai, a top executive with the Bin Zayed Group, as a member of Caduceus’s three-person advisory board.

During a meeting with his small staff, Mr. Zhou told them to point out the involvement of the Bin Zayed Group to make investors “feel comfortable,” according to material reviewed by The Times.

“Bin Zayed is definitely not stupid, right?” he said, in explaining why his staff members should mention the affiliation, according to the material.

Mr. Kidwai told The Times that he had met Mr. Zhou socially in London, but had never entered into any business with him or with Caduceus.

“It appears Mr. Zhou’s representations to investors regarding our involvement were unauthorized and materially false,” a statement from the Bin Zayed Group said.

Mr. Zhou also announced that a British pop star would perform a virtual concert using Caduceus technology, that a cricket legend had signed with the company to release digital tokens and that a rugby Hall of Famer had joined his board.

None of it came to fruition.

A spokeswoman for the rugby star, Lawrence Dallaglio, told The Times that her client did not associate with Mr. Zhou “after completing thorough due diligence.”

The Caduceus token hit the market in June 2022. The price hit its all-time high of $2.24 on July 31, 2022. It plummeted to 22 cents three weeks later and continued a downward slide. It was effectively worthless by 2024.

Investors would not get their money back. Instead of a salary, the company’s few employees had worked for options on Caduceus tokens that they would never be able to exercise. Some insiders — including Tim Bullman, the head of management — said they also had bought tokens and so lost additional money.

In January of this year, token holders were sent an email, which The Times obtained, saying that the $4 million from the initial funding round, plus $3.6 million from Mr. Tsui, were gone and the project was effectively dead.

Sara Enzen, whom Mr. Zhou hired to run a company called LightCycle in the Caduceus universe, said however much was spent, it did not go to creating a viable business.

“We had nothing to show for that money, apart from Bobby’s lifestyle,” she said.

In February 2024, an otherwise unremarkable judgment in an immigration case was posted to a court website in London.

It said that the visa of a man named Guren Zhou had expired in 2018, and that his request to remain in the country had been denied for cause: He was among several people arrested in March 2021 on suspicion of money laundering. The court decision said prosecutors had not yet decided whether to charge him.

Not long after, Mr. Zhou packed up his wife and daughter, moved to Abu Dhabi, and started a new web of companies.

He created a business called Royal Privilege Group, with a mailing address at a shared office space, offering investment services and “bespoke experiences, enhancing well-being through elegance, indulgence and memorable moments,” according to its website.

The site showed some familiar faces from his London operation, but one new name hinted at access to sovereign wealth. Abubaker Al Khoori, the chief executive of the Abu Dhabi Capital Group, the family investment office of the brother of the Emirati president, was listed as a member of Mr. Zhou’s advisory board.

In response to questions from The Times, Mr. Al Khoori said he had been invited to join the board by a mutual acquaintance, but Royal Privilege Group did not exist long enough to accomplish anything. He added that neither he nor Abu Dhabi Capital Group had provided any funds to R. P. G.

About the same time, a company that Mr. Zhou led in the Emirates took on greater significance: Web3Port, a venture fund for crypto start-ups that claimed to be partly funded by Royal Privilege Group.

Web3Port’s first major announcement was a whopper. Days after Mr. Trump’s inauguration in January 2025, the company posted on X that it had made a $10 million investment in World Liberty and was planning more.

“Both sides are committed to building a ‘long-term partnership’ and exploring opportunities in investment, ecosystem development, and more,” the post said. “We’d also like to thank @realDonaldTrump for his crypto support!”

But Web3Port had a problem lurking in the background.

The company had been the market maker, which involves setting buy and sell prices, for the token offering of another crypto company, and its role had erupted into a scandal in the industry press. By that spring, federal prosecutors in Northern California had opened an investigation into the token offering, according to court records in a civil case filed in Delaware.

Whether it was related or not, a Web3Port entity filed for a name change in the British Virgin Islands. The new name would be Aqua 1 GP Limited.

Two weeks later, Aqua 1, an entity with no public history, announced it would buy $100 million worth of World Liberty tokens. There was no mention of Mr. Zhou or Web3Port.

“Aligning with Aqua 1 validates our blueprint for global financial innovation,” Mr. Folkman, the co-founder of World Liberty, was quoted as saying in the announcement.

Arkham Intelligence, a blockchain analytics firm, eventually determined that a wallet controlled by Web3Port had purchased $20 million worth of World Liberty tokens in January and a second wallet likely controlled by Aqua 1 had purchased $80 million in June. Arkham, which added the analysis to its website, did not respond to requests for an explanation as to how it had drawn the connection.

There is some outside evidence to support Arkham’s analysis. One of the wallets it identified as controlled by Web3Port had appeared in an email from Web3Port that was obtained by CoinDesk, a crypto news site. Whoever created the wallet that Arkham linked to Aqua 1 attached the label “aqua1” to it.

Beyond the issues raised by Mr. Zhou’s history, the involvement of the Trump family would typically trigger “the highest level of regulatory scrutiny available in the financial system,” said Mr. Prinz, of Recoveris. That is because international anti-money laundering laws classify the Trumps as “politically exposed persons” with a heightened vulnerability to influence peddling, he said.

Last September, about 90 days after the World Liberty announcement, two of Mr. Zhou’s longtime employees, including a woman who had handled paying his companies’ bills for a decade, were charged in the money laundering case in London. Another defendant, speaking to a Times reporter in a courthouse hall after a hearing last month, said he had worked with Mr. Zhou during the pandemic selling masks and Covid tests.

Mr. Zhou, who had already left Britain, is the only one out of six people identified in the indictment who has not been charged. One defendant has pleaded guilty, according to court officials. Further details of the allegations have not been released. It is not clear whether prosecutors will seek Mr. Zhou’s extradition. A trial for the charged defendants is scheduled for 2028.

Mr. Zhou, meanwhile, issued more announcements, using his connections to the Trumps as a marketing point.

In September, Aqua 1 announced it had invested $20 million in a Canadian food ingredients company that was merging with a U. A. E.-based cryptocurrency company. The crypto company claims access to $1.3 billion in “sovereign wealth assets.” The announcement said Aqua 1 had “demonstrable credibility” as the largest investor in World Liberty.

It is not clear that investment happened, as the merger stalled.

In October, Mr. Zhou appeared as the chief executive of Aqua Labs, a new umbrella name for his companies, to give the opening speech at a crypto conference in Dubai.

He presented yet another new entity as a tool for trading World Liberty’s stablecoin, which is called USD1. A large image on the stage showed Mr. Trump and his three sons under the words, “The Power behind USD1” and noted that World Liberty “has both political and compliance support. USD1 is backed by the Trump family foundation WLFI.”

And in February, Mr. Zhou’s companies issued a news release announcing that Wesley K. Clark, a retired American general and former NATO supreme allied commander, would appear at an event in Abu Dhabi with Aqua Labs. The announcement called Mr. Zhou’s company “one of the largest strategic investors in the space, including a $100M investment in the governance tokens of Trump-backed World Liberty Financial.”

Mr. Zhou spoke at the event. General Clark said he did not.

General Clark said in an interview with The Times that his office had been approached about becoming involved in Mr. Zhou’s company, but that he had declined after his team learned of the money laundering investigation.

“We did a background search on him,” General Clark said, adding that his team then told Mr. Zhou’s representatives, “We’re not going to speak with you.”

Reporting was contributed by Jane Bradley, Michael Forsythe, Bradley Hope, Flávia Milhorance and Natan Odenheimer.

Russ Buettner is an investigative reporter. He has written extensively about the finances of Donald J. Trump.

Connections Coach

He spent 11 days in the Trump White House nine years ago. Now he has a hit podcast, helping the British public, among others, understand what’s going on.

Anthony Scaramucci, former White House Communications director, is the host of a podcast about American politics, “The Rest Is Politics: US.”Credit... Lexi Parra/The New York Times

Supported by

By Matt Flegenheimer

In the summer of 2017, Anthony Scaramucci was a fist-bumping, name-dropping, “front-stabbing” (his word) 53-year-old Long Island hedge funder who joined the first Trump White House as communications director against his better judgment and became Washington’s favorite suit-and-shades-wearing greaser in the precious time he had, which turned out to be a week and a half.

He spoke third-personally (“The swamp will not defeat him,” he said of himself), missed the birth of his son (while the new boss addressed Boy Scouts in West Virginia), conceded defeat to the swamp upon his firing (on Day 11) and quickly booked himself on late-night television to prove that Anthony Scaramucci — the Mooch, as he self-identified — was in on the joke of his own life.

In the summer of 2026, an ocean and approximately 11,000 news cycles away, Scaramucci is the least changed forever-changed man in politics: a fist-bumping, name-dropping, front-stabbing 62-year-old Long Island hedge funder who gets to sit inside the Royal Box at Wimbledon for reasons that still seem to astound him, mingling with high-living agents of monarchy and Benedict Cumberbatch.

He is the host of a podcast about American politics, “The Rest Is Politics: US,” with an audience that can eclipse one million per episode (much of it outside the United States) and a self-described life coach and therapist for European leaders seeking to understand President Trump, whom he now condemns.

He is touring Parliament as a distinguished guest, patiently defining the term “Long Island Guido” for the locals and grinning in fan selfies from the streets of London.

“You turned me into a vaudeville act,” Scaramucci has told Tony Pastor, a founder of Goalhanger, the British podcast company that produces his show, according to Pastor.

Scaramucci does not seem devastated by this outcome.

Co-hosted by Katty Kay, a longtime BBC journalist based in Washington, “The Rest Is Politics: US” has become one of the most influential current-affairs podcasts on the British charts, with an elite following — royals, heads of state, lawmakers, intelligence officials — among America’s nominal allies across the Western world.

The show toggles between self-flagellating introspection about political fame-seeking — “Your ego is always talking to you,” Scaramucci has counseled, second-personally — and prolific news-of-the-day take-slinging: that Trump does not actually respect excessive flattery, according to Scaramucci, even if he craves it; that Vice President JD Vance has been set up to fail from the start; that Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be wise to leave before Trump turns on him.

“That’s the Trump decoder ring, OK?” Scaramucci said of himself in a 90-minute interview at his Manhattan hedge fund office. “I know exactly how these” — his noun was unprintable, as ever — “think.”

Mr. Scaramucci’s return to political prominence is a testament to many things: the power of performative self-awareness in modern media; the durability of a certain kind of New York character from Trump 1.0 (Mr. Scaramucci, Michael Cohen, Donald J. Trump); the professional survival skills of a man who, incidentally, also sold 30 percent of his company to Sam Bankman-Fried in 2022, a few months before Mr. Bankman-Fried was exposed as a fraud. (A bobblehead in Mr. Scaramucci’s office recreates a New York Post cartoon of him commanding a sinking crypto boat, the S. S. Mooch.)

No doubt there are second acts in Trump-era American lives.

What is harder to square is this first act for Scaramucci as a major public figure on another continent.

“The whole thing is accidental,” he said, credibly.

Yet these are disorienting times with disorienting headlines, across the algae-plagued capital and the befuddled world it shapes, with zigzagging tariff pronouncements and straits that open and close.

Maybe it almost makes sense that Scaramucci — no stranger to disorienting headlines and capital plans gone mad — would evolve into one of the era’s almost-sense-making international narrators.

“Even as a Republican, the Mooch speaks to many of us on the left,” Samantha Niblett, a Labour Party politician, said by email this summer after dining with Scaramucci and showing him around Parliament, where her calls for national sex education (and a planned on-site sex-toy display) have earned her the nickname of “sex M. P.” in the British press. “He translates what’s happening.”

Pastor, the podcast executive, said that the British simply cannot understand how America reached this point politically.

“We require explanation,” he said, allowing that it was likewise preposterous to see Scaramucci watching tennis with British aristocrats. “I haven’t heard it explained better than by Anthony Scaramucci.”

It has helped that Scaramucci understands the president far more than his 11 days would imply. They were donor peers during Mitt Romney’s 2012 presidential campaign — New York rich guys who liked seeing themselves on television.

Both have a history of win-some-lose-some deal making that netted out a pile of money (though Scaramucci, the son of a crane operator, had less of a head start).

Both are veterans of reality competitions — Scaramucci has appeared on “Celebrity Big Brother” and something called “Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test.”

“Dude, you have my phones?” he asked a (female) associate at one point during the interview. “Let me show him the picture of me getting pushed out of the helicopter.”

But beneath a “Guido exoskeleton,” as he calls it, one through line in his biography had been mostly concealed.

“I have a love affair with the U. K.,” Scaramucci said.

He spent a semester at the London School of Economics during college and ran the 1992 London Marathon. He traveled there often in a career that took him from Goldman Sachs, where he overlapped with Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada (“He came to my wine party at Davos”), to a hedge fund life that exposed him to all manner of British characters (“Michael Milken introduced me to Tony Blair”).

His infamous 2017 line about “front stabbers,” which he compared favorably to Washington-style backstabbers, came in an interview with the BBC.

Even the bullpen at his office, SkyBridge Capital, where Winston Churchill’s stern visage greets employees, is decorated with wartime propaganda recovered from a London tube station.

“DESERVE VICTORY!” reads the framed sign, purchased by Scaramucci amid the global financial crisis.

“When I have a rough moment in my life, I always go out and buy something resilient-related, you know what I mean?” he said. “This guy, to me, is the symbol of resilience.”

And so, the Mooch fights on the beaches (from a home podcast space in the Hamptons).

He fights in the hills (of Davos, Switzerland).

The swamp may have defeated him, but could it really have the last word if Anthony Scaramucci never stopped talking?

Day 1 was instructive.

“I’ve seen this guy throw a dead spiral through a tire,” Scaramucci said of Trump from the White House briefing room on July 21, 2017, hastening to add (four times) that he loved the president.

“I took trial advocacy at Harvard Law School,” he volunteered in one non sequitur. “A little name-dropping there, if you don’t mind.”

He blew a little kiss on the way out.

“Purebred New Yorker,” former Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani, another Trump ally, said approvingly at the time.

Maybe that was part of the problem.

Before long, Scaramucci was going full New Yorker (while in conversation with a reporter from The New Yorker), exploring pathbreaking frontiers in profanity to disparage White House colleagues like Stephen K. Bannon and Reince Priebus.

The incoming chief of staff, John F. Kelly, did not let Scaramucci reach August.

“No WH chaos!” Trump wrote on then-Twitter the day of the firing, less than persuasively.

Scaramucci still begins some stories with flourishes like “Trump said something really funny to me once — this happened on Wednesday — I know it was a Wednesday because I was only there for one Wednesday.”

And Kelly, now a fellow Trump critic during a second Trump administration, has become a friend.

“I’m not so sure he was quite prepared for working with the Trump family,” Kelly said in an interview. “I know I wasn’t.”

By his account, Scaramucci hired a crisis communications expert upon his dismissal, ignored that expert’s advice to disappear to Tuscany for a few years, and busied himself with leveraging his peculiar new celebrity and reconciling with his Trump-averse wife, Deidre, who had filed for divorce shortly before he took the White House job.

He appeared as a host on “TMZ Live.” He ballparked his speaking fee at around $40,000. (It is now in the $50,000 to $75,000 range, his manager, Ron Xepoleas, said. “Lot of London,” he added.)

He started a podcast with Deidre, “Mooch and the Mrs.” (Scaramucci has five children from two marriages.)

He introduced a befuddling social media project called “The Scaramucci Post,” which attracted outrage after posting a Twitter survey asking how many Jews died in the Holocaust — without his knowledge, he said. (“You’ve got to have a zero-tolerance policy on Nazis,” he explained at the time.)

He became a completist in the canon of late-night sendups of Anthony Scaramucci.

“I was being called Tony Soprano on the Potomac. I was called a ‘Jersey Shore’ cast member,” he remembered. “‘Human cocaine.’ I liked that one.”

Still, Scaramucci stayed mostly loyal to the president.

After having raised money for Trump in 2016 (once his preferred candidates, Scott Walker and Jeb Bush, fell away) and assisted with the presidential transition, Scaramucci retained some affection for the administration, he said, despite his own debacle.

He was a reliable defender on Trump-skeptical cable networks like CNN and MSNBC for another two years, before declaring the president “off the rails” in August 2019.

“The honest people in the room know that he is crazy,” Scaramucci said then.

The two began tweeting mean things at each other, only enhancing Scaramucci’s reputation at those Trump-skeptical cable networks.

Unlike some apostates like Cohen, Trump’s former lawyer who has lately returned to praising him, Scaramucci has remained broadly consistent in his assessments of Trump for the last seven years, while maintaining contact with many people in the president’s orbit. (“Relationships are fluid,” he observed, accurately enough, on Cohen’s new radio program recently.)

In 2024, he endorsed Kamala Harris, marveling aloud at the oddity of an anti-Trump tent that included him, former Vice President Dick Cheney and former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio.

“Strange coalition,” de Blasio said in an interview. “But in the moment, it made sense.” (The two intersected ahead of a “Paisans for Kamala” video fund-raiser that de Blasio helped organize.)

By then, the most conspicuous legacy of Scaramucci’s White House chapter was probably a long-running bit that enshrined his surname as a unit of time.

“All right, folks, it’s 11 days out,” he said knowingly into a camera at his office last month. He was shooting a promotional video to be published on social media 11 days before the release of his coming book (“All the Wrong Moves”) about the “catastrophic decisions” that facilitated Trump’s rise.

“You’ve got one ‘Scaramucci’ left to preorder.”

During a recent visit to Britain, Scaramucci was explaining the courtship rituals of Long Island to a former Conservative member of Parliament, lapsing into what sounded like Danny Zuko fan fiction.

Wearing a gold chain with his hair blown back, Scaramucci recalled, he would do push-ups in the parking lot of a local hot spot. Once inside, if a young woman rejected him, he would return to his car, change shirts and try a fresh pickup line: “It had to be the shirt. What about now?”

“I tell you,” Scaramucci told his host, Gyles Brandreth, “that worked.”

Decades later, adjusting his political profile has not been entirely different.

The uniform might change — he is with the president; he is against the president; he is gently taunting his new supporters by celebrating America’s first president (“It’s Only Treason if You Lose,” his George Washington T-shirt read for a Fourth of July video) — but Scaramucci does not, exactly.

He has a talent for “taking the piss out of himself,” said Pastor, the podcast executive, repeating a Britishism that other admirers also invoked. And he has a way of wearing down whatever constituency he is courting.

In person, he is relentless and contradictory and plainly amusing in the way that people who know Trump (including Scaramucci) often describe the president’s private bearing.

He will say he is not one of those guys who gratuitously display famous faces in their offices before lingering on photographs of Warren Buffett, Josh Brolin and Oliver Stone (“I did ‘Wall Street 2’ with those guys”) and a framed cartoon of himself from “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert.”

He will share Tony Blair’s contact information with a reporter (when asked) and toss in a personalized copy of “From Wall Street to the White House and Back: The Scaramucci Guide to Unbreakable Resilience” (when not asked).

It is not lost on Scaramucci that he calls working for Trump the biggest mistake of his life but would register as another mostly anonymous big-money political gadfly without his Washington blip.

When Kay, a veteran BBC broadcaster with an accent to match, was looking for a podcast co-host ahead of the 2024 presidential election, she eyed Scaramucci in part because he was once an insider but also because of the strange symphony they might produce regardless of the subject.

“Podcasts are so much about voices,” Kay said. “The sound of my voice and the sound of Anthony’s voice are so different. And I couldn’t think of another podcast, particularly on politics, that had two people that sounded like that.”

Scaramucci can sound most authoritative when discussing the personal and professional incentives of those around the president, particularly when they seem to mirror his own from a former life.

After the sudden death last month of Senator Lindsey Graham, a onetime Trump antagonist who became an unbridled booster, Scaramucci recalled watching Graham, an acquaintance through the years, as Trump commandeered the party.

“Everybody in the Republican Party goes through that carousel, myself included, so I stand also accused of some of that hypocrisy,” he told Kay. “But I think it cost Lindsey in the end. I think that that was soul-tearing for Lindsey Graham.”

At his most diagnostically ambitious, Scaramucci has labeled Trump a “humiliation ritualist” who is best explained by his own insecurities or perhaps a tortured relationship with his father.

Even some who like Scaramucci have tweaked his qualifications for such appraisals.

“He made it 11 days!” said John Catsimatidis, a New York billionaire friend of the president who has known Scaramucci for years. “At least he has something to talk about for the rest of his life.”

He also has what he has always seemed to want: an audience, no matter how far-flung.

More than two-thirds of his viewers and listeners come from outside the United States, according to podcast statistics, with major followings not only in Britain but across Canada, Australia and Ireland.

“There’s only five million people, but it’s, like, the most popular political podcast in Norway,” Scaramucci said. “We had the prime minister on from Davos.”

Yet as Scaramucci has reinvented himself internationally, some America-first instincts have persisted.

After England squandered its early advantage in the World Cup semifinal, Scaramucci could not resist trolling viewers the next day with another George Washington T-shirt.

“The British,” it read, beneath Scaramucci’s perma-smirk, “Blew a 13 Colony Lead.”

Anthony Scaramucci was a very public figure for a very short time nine years ago. He worked for 11 heady days as President Trump’s finger-gunning, sound-biting, late-night-comedy-inspiring White House communications director before being summarily fired. He now calls working for Trump the biggest mistake of his career. So what could Scaramucci possibly have to say, all this time later, about a president who remains perplexing to much of the Western world? Quite a bit, actually. We try to make sense of Scaramucci’s re-reinvention as a big-in-Europe podcaster who tries to make sense of American politics for an audience that remains pretty baffled by all of this.

Matt Flegenheimer is a correspondent for The Times focusing on in-depth profiles of powerful figures.

Connections Coach

Employees say the performing arts center’s quirky-looking mice have an exotic back story. Do they?

Skittles, a mouse that has made a home at the Kennedy Center, was nicknamed by stagehands. Credit... Colleen Shannon

Supported by

By Elizabeth Williamson

Elizabeth Williamson reported from a favorite rodent rendezvous at the Kennedy Center.

President Trump’s takeover of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has left the building nearly empty. So the few lonely staff members who remain ahead of a potential two-year closure this month for renovations are prone to sharing tales of what for 50 years has made the place special.

Like the mice.

Kennedy Center mice do not resemble the typical gray house mice found in fields and woods in warmer weather and in kitchens and attics when it’s cold. They are roughly half that size, with large ears and fur of a golden tan color that, if they were horses, would be called palomino. Their bellies are pearl white.

For years stagehands have spotted a tan mouse — or maybe alternating mice — sitting motionless beneath a wheelchair ramp facing one of the center’s two Millennium Stages, seemingly watching the evening shows. Over the holidays in 2024, the mice devoured a fancy charcuterie board that the cast of the Broadway musical “& Juliet” left out overnight in the Opera House.

The mice have also nosed their way into reviews of Kennedy Center performances. In 2018, what The Washington Post called a “baby mouse” lingered in the Concert Hall during a National Symphony Orchestra performance of Tchaikovsky’s “Francesca da Rimini.” The mouse ran for the prime seats near the stage and “scurried around 12 or more rows near the left aisle, forcing audience members to move their coats and bags as they struggled to remain quiet and still,” a Post arts reporter, Peggy McGlone, wrote.

In May, Oussama Zahr noted in his New York Times review of the symphony’s concert version of Puccini’s “Il Trittico” that a mouse “scampered through the orchestra seats, startling some audience members.”

An usher told Mr. Zahr that of course the center’s mice were drawn to the Italian masterwork. Puccini runs in their blood.

In the quiet of the center’s Grand Foyer last month, four stagehands paused from cleaning the rigging over the idled Millennium Stage to share the story of the mice.

The Kennedy Center was built as a living memorial to the slain President John F. Kennedy, a patron of the arts who championed its construction. Amid a surge of grief and tribute after his assassination in 1963, more than 60 nations donated furnishings and artwork to the center rising on the Potomac.

The largest of these gifts came from Italy: 3,700 tons of dazzling white Carrara marble for the facade and interior walls, specially mined in Tuscany’s Apuan Alps, in the same area as the marble for Michelangelo’s David. The region is home to the Alpine field mouse and its genetic kin.

For decades Kennedy Center workers have insisted that a few of these Italian rodents traveled to Washington in the late 1960s, nestled in crates carrying the marble shipments.

“We’ve talked to the pest guys that come through and set all the mousetraps and they’re like, ‘This is the only place in D. C. that has these,’” said Thomas Benya, the head electrician in the Eisenhower Theater, referring to the tiny tan mice.

The pest guys work at a contractor called American Pest, which declined to comment.

The marble was unpacked and installed between 1968 and 1970, and legend holds that descendants of the Carrara stowaways have been living large in the performing arts center ever since.

“The person who told me the story was a stagehand who was here for the opening of this place,” said Annemarie Mountjoy, the chief electrician in the Opera House.

Early last year, Colleen Shannon, who handles lighting in the center’s Family Theater, captured a fleeting image of a reddish tan mouse with her phone, and the stagehands nicknamed it Skittles. This spring, “I had one run across my console while I was running a show,” she said.

“They’re just cute as the dickens,” she said. “So tiny. The cockroaches are bigger.”

Staff members have swapped photos and tales of the mice for years, the stagehands said. Although Washington’s many universities and science and research institutions make it a virtual nest of mammalian expertise, no one they knew of had checked out the story.

Maurizio Bufalini ran a quarry in Carrara, Italy, that supplied marble for the Kennedy Center. The contract is a source of pride in the family, which has been in the stone business for more than 300 years. Mr. Bufalini’s son Alberto took over the business, now called Bufalini Marmi, after he died in 1998.

The Bufalinis have supplied marble to a number of notable American structures, including for the marble interior of the World Trade Center towers that were destroyed in the Sept. 11, 2001, attack. In the 1950s through the 1970s, Bufalini was a favored supplier of marble to structures designed by Edward Durell Stone, the Kennedy Center architect.

“Of course we have mice here” in the factory, Mr. Bufalini, 58, said in a phone interview last week.

In the late 1960s, the company quarried and packed the slabs of marble, each roughly 8 feet by 4 feet and 5 inches thick, into wooden shipping crates. Straw was used for cushioning. Each container held 2,200 to 3,300 pounds, meaning more than 3,000 crates of marble crossed the Atlantic headed for the Kennedy Center. The journey took from three weeks to a month.

In the wild the Alpine field mouse and its kin live on insects, plants and seeds, all potentially available in packing straw. It has adapted to its arid environment by extracting water from its food in a metabolic process that allows it to survive for long periods without drinking.

“When we import stone from other countries, for sure you can find insects or a little creature that has been trapped inside the container,” Mr. Bufalini said.

“It is a funny story, and it’s also possible but difficult to verify. You could see if the mice eat pasta or not.”

I took the case to Joel Sartore, who photographed the Alpine field mouse at the Czech Republic’s Plzen Zoo, famous for its rodent collection. Mr. Sartore is a photographer and founder of the Photo Ark, a National Geographic-supported effort to document all the planet’s animals. He works with a network of biologists to identify species he finds in the wild, and so he emailed Ms. Shannon’s photo of Skittles to Sandra Sneckenberger, a mouse specialist at the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

She responded to Mr. Sartore within an hour. The blurry photo made it hard to tell whether the mouse is an Italian field mouse or the local, less exotic white-footed mouse.

“All we need is a skull of a dead one, to look at the teeth, though,” Ms. Sneckenberger wrote.

Mr. Sartore was game. “Maybe someone in maintenance there knows of one sitting on someone’s desk?” Mr. Sartore suggested. “Some folks love to save skulls for some reason. I see them of all sizes in zoo manager offices.”

Ian Millholland, an electrician in the Opera House who does double duty cleaning out the mouse traps, did not respond to a text message asking whether there were any skulls sitting on desks in the Kennedy Center.

Darrin Lunde, mammal collection manager at the Smithsonian Institution’s Museum of Natural History, seemed like the best Washington expert to consult. He has documented more than a dozen new species, including two of the New Guinea water rat, and shed new light on hundreds more on expeditions he led in the Americas, Africa and Southeast Asia.

“It’s a little far-fetched that only in the Kennedy Center do they have these mice,” he said upon hearing the story. “It’s like Big Foot. People want to believe in something special.”

Then he reviewed Ms. Shannon’s photo of Skittles.

“It is intriguing,” he said, noting the animal’s “orangey” color. “It’s much too small to be a white-footed mouse or a deer mouse from the local population.”

“If it’s anything interesting it’s going to be one of the three or four species of Apodemus living in Italy,” he added, using the Latin name for the mouse’s genus. “It does look like an Apodemus to me, but I’m not saying definitively that’s what it is.

“If we could get a specimen in hand, it’s not out of the question,” he said.

But back at the Kennedy Center the stagehands said the mice, like the people, had grown scarce. None appeared in the Eisenhower Theater break room one day last month, despite a full trash bin. The Family Theater, Skittles’s haunt, was likewise quiet.

Last month, Mr. Millholland checked the traps. Empty. Referring to the delectable missing bait in some of them, “They know how to chew off the peanut butter,” he said.

Maybe the story of the mice, treasured lore in a place with an uncertain future, would wind up too difficult to prove. Or too good to check.

“I don’t want to know,” Ms. Shannon said.

Dylan Freedman contributed research from Washington.

Elizabeth Williamson is a feature writer for The Times, based in Washington. She has been a journalist for three decades, on three continents.

A Democrat Sounds the Alarm on Christian Nationalism in Congress

The New York Times August 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Q & A

Representative Jared Huffman of California, the only self-declared “humanist” in Congress, writes in a new book that the separation of church and state is in grave danger.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from the Capitol

Representative Jared Huffman, Democrat of California, thought he was going to make himself a political pariah when he announced publicly that he did not believe in God.

Mr. Huffman, the only self-declared “humanist” in Congress, found that constituents in his mostly liberal Northern California district were unfazed.

Now Mr. Huffman has written a book in which he takes on how religion influences politics in America, in which he argues that extreme Christian nationalism, embraced and enabled by influential Republicans, is the country’s most dangerous political movement. He also accuses many of his own Democratic colleagues of being “incapable” of naming and confronting the threat.

In “No Prophets: The Fight to Save Democracy From Christian Nationalism,” which is to be published this month, Mr. Huffman, who grew up in the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, an offshoot of Mormonism, argues that the rise of Christian nationalism in American politics is openly targeting democracy, church-state separation and pluralism.

Ahead of the book's release, Mr. Huffman spoke to The New York Times about his colleagues, his atheism, his distrust of the pastors in the halls of the Capitol and his argument that Speaker Mike Johnson is a Christian nationalist who dangerously blurs the boundary between church and state. The speaker, who has placed his evangelical Christianity at the center of his political life and policy positions, did not respond to a request for comment about the book's claims.

The interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

You write that you’re the only member of Congress “dumb enough to publicly admit I don’t believe in God,” but discovered that doing so did not cost you politically. Can you explain why?

All conventional wisdom would suggest it’s a dumb idea to admit it. Everyone I consulted with said it was a dumb idea. There’s an assumption that there’s a huge stigma against nonbelievers, and the polling backs that up.

But when I came out, the backlash never happened. I have a district that is progressive, well-educated and doesn’t much care about anyone’s religious label.

I tried to make it very clear that I’m not judging anyone else’s religion, I’m not suggesting mine is better than yours, or that I want everyone to be a humanist like me. I was just tired of ducking the question, and I wanted people to know what my personal moral framework is.

You write that former Representative Liz Cheney, Republican of Wyoming, deliberately erased references to Christian nationalism from the Jan. 6 committee report, even though it played a visible role in the mob attack on the Capitol. You argue that she didn’t want to be branded as “anti-Christian.” [Ms. Cheney did not respond to a request for comment about the claims.] What happened to that part of the report?

Former Representative Adam Kinzinger, Republican of Illinois [and a member of the Jan. 6 committee], was very cleareyed that Fox News would jump on this and try to use it to disparage the entire report. But he suggested that with enough of a disclaimer — and by explaining that telling this story is important, doing it in a way that’s clear you’re not trashing Christianity, you’re just being honest about the radicalization and mobilization and the ethos of this riot — there was a way to do that.

It’s deep-sixed. Drafts were not kept. That’s another mystery here. I don’t know if that was the chaos of rushing to finish this report or if there was a deliberate, “don’t leave incomplete work product” edict. Nobody had copies.

You write that after Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, joked about your “right to not worship God” during a caucus meeting, several “closeted nonbelievers” told you, “if only he knew how many of us there are.” How many of you are there?

In the country writ large, according to the latest polling, 30 percent are nonreligious. Not all of those are open atheists, but a lot of them are. I think the Democratic caucus is not far-off from that.

On the Republican side, you have a monolith of Christianity, with one or two very conservative or Orthodox Jews allowed to ride along. I have a hard time believing all of them are devout. I think there’s probably a lot of fakers and nonbelievers in those ranks, too. But that’s where there really would be a career-ending penalty if someone were to be honest about it.

Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, Democrat of Washington, has said she is the only Democrat who attends a Republican Bible study and she told me once, “I feel like my party is embarrassed I’m a Christian.” You write that you’re embarrassed that strategists in your party advise lawmakers to act more publicly religious to compete for the Christian vote. Who is right?

I would be embarrassed to go to that Bible study.

Ralph Drollinger, the founder of Capitol Ministries, used to lead weekly Bible studies for elected officials, and he is the most extreme of the extremes. He should be an absolute pariah, but he’s a total V. I. P. in Trump’s Washington. The fact that a very small number of Democrats play along with that, I find pretty disturbing. He’s against women’s rights and he has these Bible studies where he tells cabinet officials what God wants them to do with their power.

[Mr. Drollinger denied that he does not believe in women’s rights and described himself as a “historic evangelical expositor of scripture” who believes “in accurately stating the authorial intent of the Bible — not my own opinions.”]

Marie Perez was on a letter inviting people to one. It’s rabid right-wing stuff. I’m not suggesting that she believes the same stuff as Drollinger, but you’re lending bipartisan credence to a really dangerous extremist, and I don’t think that’s OK.

[Ms. Perez, who noted that Mr. Drollinger himself did not lead the study she attended or insert his personal views into it, responded: “As a Christian and a Democrat, I think it’s profoundly important to reject the idea that I can’t worship alongside people who have different political ideas than me. My faith doesn’t tell me to put up walls; it tells me to build a ladder.”]

How should Democrats compete for the Christian vote?

Democrats should learn to talk more about religious liberty instead of just religion. Democrats have somehow managed to make both religious people and nonbelievers feel unwelcome by their awkwardness in discussing the basic concept of religious liberty, which doesn’t exist without church-state separation.

I feel so good about James Talarico, [the Democrat running for Senate in Texas], and Senator Raphael Warnock, [Democrat of Georgia and senior pastor at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta], as messengers on this. They talk about their faith authentically without trying to harness the coercive power of government to impose it on anyone.

You write about pastors lurking in the Capitol like lobbyists, intercepting members en route to votes and inviting them to Bible studies. I have not been aware of this.

They’re all over the place, handing out pocket cards to get you to their Bible study. Then they use their proximity to power both to influence members of Congress and staff and go back to their congregations and raise money.

I certainly feel uncomfortable with it, because I know that some of them are not just there to pray with members of Congress, they’re there to drive an agenda. They’re trying to push religious doctrine into our laws and policies and institutions. That’s crossing a line.

You write that Speaker Mike Johnson is dangerously promoting Christian nationalism. But he has had trouble getting things done. Is he effective or inept?

He has been hapless and ineffective at governing. But if you judge him by, “Has he advanced the cause of Christian nationalism?” he’s been wildly successful. He elevated the Congressional Prayer Breakfast into Statuary Hall; he instituted a new National Gathering for Prayer and Repentance where members go over to the Museum of the Bible and repent for national sins like abortion.

He allows a pastor he is close with to bring hundreds of pastors multiple times a year to hear a whitewashed version of American history that is rampant Christian nationalism. People need to understand that as incompetent as he is at governing, he has been powerful and very effective in advancing this Christian nationalist movement.

After Republicans passed the “Big, Beautiful Bill,” Johnson did an interview in the chapel and claimed he had been down on his knees praying every day. He said the passage of this bill was God’s will and God’s plan. There are so many of these things, each of them standing alone might feel like not much. But when you take it together, I feel that the wall of separation is in real trouble.

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

Inside the War on Hezbollah’s Finances

The New York Times August 09, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Israel and the United States aren’t just targeting the Lebanese militant group’s weapons. They’re going after its money.

By Euan WardEric SchmittRonen Bergman and Hwaida Saad

Euan Ward reviewed internal banking documents and emails and, with the reporting team, spoke with dozens of Lebanese, U. S., Israeli and Hezbollah officials.

When Israel launched its latest war against Hezbollah in March, the first targets the military warned it would strike were not weapons depots or underground command centers.

They were banks.

Israeli fighter jets leveled more than a dozen branches of a shadowy financial institution known as Al-Qard al-Hassan, long accused of operating as Hezbollah’s bank in Lebanon. More airstrikes followed on exchange shops that Iran used to funnel money to Hezbollah, its Lebanese proxy, and on gas stations that generated revenue for the group.

With these strikes, Israel was sending a clear message: Hezbollah’s money, not only its arsenal, was in the cross hairs.

The bombings capped the most aggressive campaign yet by Israel, the Trump administration and Lebanon’s own government to squeeze Hezbollah financially by disrupting the group’s funding channels, particularly from Iran.

For months leading up to the war, Lebanon’s government, under pressure from the Trump administration, worked to choke off the routes that the group used to receive and move money, such as Beirut’s international airport. Washington also pressed the Lebanese central bank to tighten controls over the country’s cash economy, which Hezbollah had long exploited.

Now, Hezbollah is grappling with its most severe economic strain in years, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times and interviews with Lebanese, U. S. and Israeli officials and Hezbollah insiders. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity, citing confidential intelligence assessments, diplomatic protocol or fear of retribution.

The war that began in March was the second in less than three years between Israel and Hezbollah, one of the world’s most heavily armed militias. In the previous conflict, which began in late 2023, Israel killed Hezbollah’s longtime leader, Hassan Nasrallah, along with many other top figures in the movement.

Seizing that moment, leaders in Washington and Israel sensed that Hezbollah was vulnerable and coordinated their efforts to clamp down on its funding. They went after the financial networks that had long underpinned the group’s power, while also turning up the pressure on Lebanon’s government to disarm Hezbollah.

While the wars with Hamas in Gaza and Iran have drawn global attention, the financial squeeze on Hezbollah represents a quieter front in a campaign by Washington and Israel aimed at crippling Tehran’s ability to project power through its proxy militias across the Middle East.

Founded in 1982, Hezbollah has long stood as the crown jewel of that network.

The group’s finances are secretive, and the full extent to which the crackdown has affected its vast operations remains unclear. Both Hezbollah and its chief backer, Iran, have also proven resilient in the face of the efforts to weaken them, able to bounce back militarily and to find new ways to keep the money flowing.

Nevertheless, Hezbollah is struggling to finance its sprawling social welfare network, which has long underpinned its support among its Shiite Muslim base in Lebanon. The group has also increasingly prioritized military spending after Israel’s offensives took a heavy toll on its capabilities.

Hezbollah’s chief spokesman, Youssef al-Zein, told The New York Times in May that the group had halted the compensation payments it had pledged to supporters as it struggles to meet the needs of hundreds of thousands of people displaced by the war.

The State Department estimated before the war that Iran’s funding to Hezbollah was about $700 million per year, providing a majority of the group’s billion-dollar annual budget. Iran has increased its financial support for Hezbollah over the past year, according to Lebanese, U. S. and Israeli officials, but the money is still not enough to cover Hezbollah’s considerable war-related expenses.

“The scale of the battle’s demands and the displacement have placed significant burdens on Hezbollah,” Mr. al-Zein said. As a result, “resources are being managed according to priority,” he added. “There is undoubtedly pressure, but Hezbollah is able to overcome it.”

The crackdown on Hezbollah’s finances began in earnest in late 2024. Soon after a U. S.-mediated cease-fire halted the Israel-Hezbollah war, the sudden fall of the dictator Bashar al-Assad’s regime in neighboring Syria left the group more isolated than ever from Tehran.

Hezbollah had lost a crucial smuggling route at precisely the moment it needed money to rebuild and sustain its operations.

For decades, Hezbollah oversaw a state within a state in Lebanon — one that fed, housed and paid its loyal followers. It built a media network, established hospitals and schools, drew revenue from gas stations and pharmaceutical companies and amassed an arsenal more powerful than the state’s own military with Iran’s financial backing.

But when the Syrian land route into Lebanon was effectively severed, Iran scrambled to find other methods to finance the group, according to U. S. and Israeli officials and people familiar with Hezbollah’s finances.

Iran turned to Beirut’s airport, which for years had effectively operated under Hezbollah’s control and was used to receive Iranian funding and arms, according to a U. S. official and a senior Lebanese official briefed on the matter.

But U. S. and Israeli officials were on that trail.

Early last year, U. S. officials relayed an Israeli warning to Lebanon’s government. Iran was sending suitcases stuffed with U. S. dollars to Hezbollah on civilian flights to Beirut — in some cases carried by Iranian diplomats — according to two Lebanese officials and an Israeli official. U. S. officials declined to comment. The warning led Lebanon to suspend all flights from Iran, a measure that remains in place.

Hezbollah-affiliated airport staff were also removed from their roles, and the Lebanese authorities installed security officers who work in coordination with American officials, according to a U. S. official and two Lebanese officials.

When Ali Larijani, Iran’s national security chief, visited Lebanon last August, his meeting with Prime Minister, Nawaf Salam, showed just how much had changed inside the country.

“Our message to the Iranians was very clear,” Mr. Salam said in an interview with The Times not long after the visit. “We cannot allow the Iranians to interfere in our domestic affairs,” he added.

“This wasn’t music to their ears,” he said.

Mr. Larijani was killed months later in the U. S.-Israel war with Iran.

Washington then turned its sights on Lebanon’s central bank, an opaque institution that had long operated with little scrutiny. Lebanon operates on a largely cash-based economy, which the U. S. Treasury Department says Hezbollah has exploited to launder illicit funds and funnel money from Iran.

Last year, the Trump administration worked to influence the appointment of a new Lebanese central bank governor, according to a senior Lebanese official briefed on the process. U. S. administration officials did not respond to requests for comment on their role.

The new governor, Karim Souaid, quickly proved himself willing to move against Hezbollah. He sidelined or fired top bank officials suspected of ties to the group, ordering his office swept for listening devices and refusing to use bank-issued computers amid fears of surveillance, according to a senior central bank official and an internal memo obtained by The Times.

The central bank did not respond to a request for comment.

With the new U. S.-backed governor in place, the central bank started an investigation into the country’s largest money service businesses and their suspected use by Hezbollah to move funds, according to internal documents seen by The Times and the senior central bank official. Since the investigation began, the Lebanese authorities have tightened oversight of money transfers.

“Hezbollah was able to continuously generate substantial amounts of money through the abuse of those networks,” Brian E. Nelson, a former top Treasury official who oversaw sanctions on the group under the Biden administration, said in an interview.

Hezbollah’s media office called the claims that it had exploited Lebanon’s cash-based economy “false and entirely baseless.”

As large money service businesses came under greater scrutiny, Hezbollah continued to rely heavily on a less regulated network of exchange houses, which has rapidly become the primary channel through which Iran finances the group, according to a senior Israeli defense official and another person familiar with Hezbollah’s finances.

The funds move from Iran through the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Iraq using hawala, an informal system of broker-to-broker transfers without the underlying cash necessarily crossing borders, these two people said.

When the U. S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions on Lebanese money exchangers in last November, it said Iran had already funneled around $1 billion to Hezbollah that year, largely through the hawala method.

Hassan Moukalled, an exchanger whom the Treasury Department imposed sanctions on and described as a “key Hezbollah financial adviser,” told The Times that the international pressure had made it harder to move money but that Hezbollah was adapting.

“In a country like Lebanon, where there’s a large amount of cash, there are always possibilities,” he said.

As the crackdown picked up speed, Hezbollah’s welfare system began to show signs of strain. Hezbollah officials and beneficiaries told The Times that while salaries are largely still being paid to its tens of thousands of fighters, some social services have been rolled back as the group triages its spending.

Hezbollah has tried to drum up cash where it can.

In February, weeks before the latest Israel-Hezbollah war began, the Treasury Department said that senior officials from Al-Qard al-Hassan, Hezbollah’s de facto bank, had established a chain of gold-trading companies to raise cash. Ledgers reviewed by The Times and assessments by analysts who track Hezbollah’s cash economy indicated that gold sales have climbed over the past year.

One reason Hezbollah wanted to turn gold into cash was that Israeli airstrikes had destroyed much of Hezbollah’s foreign currency and gold reserves, according to Israeli and U. S. officials.

Last year, Lebanon barred the country’s banks and brokerages from dealing with Al-Qard al-Hassan, further isolating Hezbollah from the formal financial system.

Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese people, many of them Hezbollah supporters, rely on Al-Qard al-Hassan for interest-free loans and war-related compensation payments. The organization describes itself as a charitable lending association rather than a bank, and its director has said that Hezbollah maintains separate organizational finances.

Still, the Trump administration is now pushing Lebanon’s government to shutter it altogether.

Hassan, a taxi driver from southern Lebanon whose daughter was married to a Hezbollah fighter killed during the recent wars, said that although she was still receiving the stipend earmarked for families of slain fighters, the organization is no longer covering some medical procedures. Like thousands of supporters whose homes were destroyed, Hassan said he was still waiting on promised financial support.

After the 2024 war, Hezbollah said Al-Qard al-Hassan would distribute $12,000 to $14,000 per household to families whose homes were destroyed. But those compensation payments, repeatedly delayed, have now been halted entirely, according to the Hezbollah spokesman, Mr. al-Zein.

“They are totally silent,” Hassan said.

Aaron Boxerman, Dayana Iwaza and Patrick Kingsley contributed reporting.

Euan Ward is a Times reporter covering Lebanon and Syria. He is based in Beirut.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U. S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Ronen Bergman is a staff writer for The New York Times Magazine, based in Tel Aviv.

Forget the East Wing. The Real Demolition Has Only Just Begun.

The New York Times August 09, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Paul Goldberger

Mr. Goldberger is a former architecture critic for The Times and The New Yorker and the author of “Why Architecture Matters.”

The proposed “Arc de Trump” in Washington is less a monument than a gaudy construction the height of a skyscraper — a travesty that, if built, would dramatically change the landscape of the nation’s capital. This is probably why President Trump is so eager to get it made as fast as he can. It would be an unavoidable monument to a presidency and a man whom many Americans would rather not honor so conspicuously, if at all. He understands that once it is there, it will be hard to for anyone to make it go away.

Change is supposed to happen slowly and carefully in Washington, and there are systems in place to make that so. When the National Park Service said last week that the arch would not only block the vista between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery but would also have an impact on 35 other Washington landmarks, it was a distressing preview of the administration’s attitude toward historic preservation. The Trump administration is in the process of making it much easier to demolish historic buildings and landscapes not just in Washington but nationwide.

The Park Service’s observations were made during a Section 106 review, which has been one of our most effective historic preservation tools for the past 60 years. The name is a reference to a clause in the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. It requires that before approval is granted for any project that uses federal funds or could affect buildings or landscapes in the National Register of Historic Places, its impact on historic places must be evaluated and the public must be consulted. The Trump administration recently proposed changes that would render this type of review process impotent. If the changes go forward, the wanton destructiveness behind the arch and the East Wing ballroom will be just the beginning.

Section 106 has had a superb record of encouraging negotiation and compromise. It does not forbid change or even demolition, but it stipulates that efforts must be made to “avoid, minimize or mitigate” any harm to historic places. The very reasonableness of the law may be exactly what has led the Trump administration to be so determined to get rid of it. In the past few years in New York, Section 106 reviews have been a part of the process that has led to the saving of the T. W. A. terminal at Kennedy International Airport as well as the conversion of a portion of city’s main post office into the Moynihan Train Hall.

The proposed changes to Section 106 were issued by the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation. This is yet another of our government’s review organizations that has been filled with Trump appointees who have no sympathy for the subject on which they are expected to pass judgment. While the proposed changes do not technically eliminate Section 106, they eviscerate it.

If this new policy is enacted, it would extend the autocratic decision-making of Trump’s Washington fiascos to historic buildings and sites anywhere in the country. It is ironic indeed for the government to commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday by embarking on what Brent Leggs, the chief executive of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, has called “an unprecedented and deliberate attack on our civic and cultural inheritance.”

The Trump administration’s revised version of Section 106 replaces “the views of the public are essential to informed Federal decision making” with a statement that says the government will have “exclusive discretion to determine the usefulness of public participation” — in effect saying that federal agencies can do as they please.

The Commission on Fine Arts, the National Park Service and the National Capital Planning Commission received tens of thousands of public comments on the ballroom and the the arch, almost all of which were negative. The commissions approved both projects anyway.

The proposed changes also state that Section 106 applies only to sites that contain actual buildings and other structures, eliminating any obligation to take public input into account in cases where natural landscapes, including the sacred lands of Native Americans, are potentially compromised. A clause requiring that Section 106 reviews begin at an early stage of design has been eliminated, making it all but impossible to suggest that a project’s site be shifted to protect something historic. The bar for defining the negative impact of a project is raised much higher. One potential new clause says that federal personnel no longer need to visit threatened sites; another clause states that any proposed mitigation of negative impact must be “technically and economically feasible.” In other words, all the government has to say is, sorry, we’ve decided it will be too expensive to run that new highway through a route that will protect a cherished natural vista. Or that it just doesn’t want to be bothered.

Over the past year, we have seen the effects of Mr. Trump’s attitudes about urban planning and historic preservation. The proposed arch will destroy the vista connecting Lincoln to the Civil War dead, a space that for more than a hundred years has been kept open as one of the capital’s most subtle acts of monumental beauty. There is also the wreck that has been made of the Reflecting Pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial and the bronze statues that have been painted in gold, using funds taken from the National Park Service budget.

And let’s not forget Mr. Trump’s insistence on painting the gray granite Eisenhower Executive Office Building a stark white to have it “match” the White House. The building is arguably the greatest work of architecture of the Second Empire style left in the United States, but when the mansard roofs and columns and terraces are all bright white it will look cheap, and worse, it will be effectively ruined. Granite is not porous, so it does not hold paint. I doubt that you can find a single painted Second Empire building in Paris, and for good reason. Does anyone think the Paris Opera would look better with a coat of white paint?

Mr. Trump’s disregard for historic preservation goes back at least as far as his reneging on a promise to donate (rather than destroy) the Art Deco bas-reliefs on the facade of Bonwit Teller, which he knocked down to build Trump Tower. He got away with that. The U. S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled last Friday that he should have gotten congressional approval for his White House ballroom, likely leaving it up to the Supreme Court.

If the Trump administration succeeds in making its proposed changes to Section 106, it will take a wrecking ball to the historic preservation movement in the United States. And its effects will be felt across the country for generations.

Paul Goldberger is a former architecture critic for The Times and The New Yorker and the author of “Why Architecture Matters.”
